#5350. Team Themes: How to Divvy Up the Tasks (or Not!)

Editor’s Note: Team Themes is a periodic news feature where we ask team leaders for detailed information about how they structure and organize their teams and how they achieve success for all members.

While you might think standard operating procedure for real estate team leaders is to operate under rigid weekly calendars, those in the field are proving there is no single blueprint for success.

In fact, a closer look at three mid-sized real estate teams reveals a sharp divide: Some leaders outright reject the traditional top-down weekly schedule entirely, opting instead for individual accountability or tech-driven workflows, while another takes a more traditional approach.

With each finding different ways to fuel growth, we asked three top team leaders with six to 26 agents to pull back the curtain on their operations and share their process for divvying up the daily tasks.

Do you and your team have a set weekly schedule for business-building tasks? Why or why not?

For example, do you have set days and/or times or team members who call clients and prospects, post to social media, work on lead-gen, marketing, etc.? How are the various responsibilities of the team divided? Are any set activities scheduled for certain days of the week?

John Turner, Team Lead, Turner Victory Team at Onward Real Estate Number of team members: 12 agents Region served: Murfreesboro, Tennessee https://turnervictory.com/about-murfreesboro-real-estate-team

The short answer is no. We do not run a rigid weekly schedule for business-building tasks across the whole team. Here’s why.

Years ago, we held weekly team training. Over time, we realized our brokerage already offers extensive training, so we were mostly repeating what they provide. Now we only schedule training when we spot a specific area that needs work. That keeps training useful and keeps everyone’s time focused on what matters.

Most of our team consists of experienced agents, and many have been with us for 10 years or more. They know how to do this job. What we found was that the skill was there, but the consistency was not. A group schedule was not going to fix that, so we moved to monthly one-on-one meetings with each agent. In those meetings we talk about their goals, where they are today and what habits will keep them moving forward. Each agent builds their own routine for calling past clients and staying in touch with their sphere, and we supportively hold them accountable.

The other key piece is access. Every agent on our team knows that Tracy (my wife and co-team leader) and I are easy to reach. They can come to us with a question, ask for advice or just brainstorm an idea. Sometimes the best training occurs when the agent is actively involved in a transaction and runs into an issue. Therefore, it’s important they know they have a trusted mentor who can help them walk through that deal.

For team leaders building a team, my advice is to match your structure to the people you have. A newer team may need a tight daily schedule. A seasoned team often needs accountability and an available mentor.

Read more about how Turner turned data and trust into ChatGPT referrals here.

Chris Colgan, Founder and CEO, Colgan Team Number of members: 26 agents Region served: Northern Virginia and Metro D.C. https://www.colganteam.com/

Monday through Friday, we have a morning huddle from 9 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. I check in on everybody’s calls, what their plan is for the day, and what’s happening in the market in real-time. We talk about what’s positive, sometimes watch a motivational video, and work through role-playing or real situations agents are dealing with.

I’m still in the thick of it, selling just like they are. So when I talk about a buyer getting cold feet, an inspection negotiation or a listing that isn’t getting showings, it’s not just something I read about. It’s something I’m dealing with, too.

Every Tuesday, we also have a required in-office meeting from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.

Outside of those meetings, I expect agents to block 90 minutes every weekday for calls and follow-up. Start with your hot leads and new leads. Talk to the people who are on the fence and figure out what’s keeping them from moving forward. Our expectation is 10 real conversations a day, lasting at least two minutes, tracked in Brivity or Follow Up Boss.

I tell them, “If you don’t have 90 minutes a day to call people, you need to ask yourself whether you’re making time for this business.” Saturday and Sunday, you’re out showing houses and doing open houses. You need to be having those conversations during the week.

We also use an AI assistant that emails each agent their top 10 leads to call that morning. It points them toward training through PLACE or Real based on where they need help. Maybe they’re struggling with scripts. Maybe they need help running an open house. The idea is to give them direction, not just tell them to work harder.

On the marketing side, I handle most of it because I genuinely love it. YouTube, Instagram, Google, listing marketing—that’s where I spend a lot of my time. We put out three YouTube videos a week, which is a lot of work. I’d estimate we’ve had around 40 to 50 closings from YouTube and Instagram this year.

But agents still need to build their own visibility. I tell them to post three valuable things on Facebook every day: being out with a client, showing a house, giving useful real estate advice. Your friends and family are already there. Let them see that you’re actually doing the work.

I also tell agents they should be doing three open houses a week in this market. Does every agent do that? No. I wish they did. We use QR codes for sign-ins and track the activity, but getting someone to sign in is only the beginning. Some agents do the open house and then don’t follow up properly. I do follow up, and it’s a huge lead source. You can’t put in the time to meet all those buyers and then never call them.

We have transaction coordinators, listing coordination and support staff who help agents manage their databases and stay on top of things in Slack. Our operations manager handles onboarding and offboarding. We’re constantly recruiting, but we’re also honest when someone isn’t a fit. You can be a good person and still not want to work the way our team expects.

The hardest part isn’t putting a schedule together. It’s getting people to follow it consistently. We track the activity, check in and have direct conversations when someone isn’t doing the work. Does everybody execute perfectly every week? No. That’s something we’re always working on.

I keep telling the team: “This is not a dabbler market. It’s the full immersion season.” That means making the calls, following up, showing up to meetings with your camera on, being out with clients and doing the activities even when you don’t feel like it. The schedule gives us a way to turn that expectation into something people can actually follow.

Read more about how Colgan turned a passion for sneakers into a successful real estate career here.

Phil Sexton, Founder, HomeSmart NEXT Team Number of team members: Six, with four agents Region served: Scottsdale, Arizona https://nextrealestate.team/ A. No. NEXT Team members assign weekly tasks to us, not the other way around. HomeSmart NEXT is not a classic “Last Name Team” that the industry is used to. We’re the nerds in the back office. We’re like a CTO and CMO for our agents, allowing them to be the most technologically advanced real estate marketers in the industry…without having to build the tech. Most agents want to leverage AI, but they don’t want to become a techno-nerd. Our dashboard is growing with the AI tools to choose from for marketing, prospecting, advertising and operations. If they learn about something new or cool in a class, they ask us for it, and we build it. It really is an amazing time to be in business. Read more about how Sexton is rethinking the agent team concept here.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5349. He sold Bibles door to door. Now he runs a 35,000-home luxury exchange club in 103 countries

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

#5348. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

That shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

#5347. Paychecks are growing, but buyers are still falling behind

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

The October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

The gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

At October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

#5346. Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data

Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data company, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.

A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the company develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company said it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.

The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The company said it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.

The company was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.

“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”

The company said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.

“Most AI agents today piece together their picture of a patient from text, one question at a time,” said co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Ming Yang “Max” Lu, Ph.D. “We’re building a native representation of each patient’s multimodal, longitudinal history that powers prediction and analysis across an entire population.”

Aevius said the capital from the round would support continued research and development of its foundation models and expand the company’s engineering, clinical and commercial teams.

The company is bringing its technology to health systems at large. That means advancing clinical research and reach, anticipating patient needs, and informing care delivery and resource planning.

On the insurance side, catching disease earlier means fewer visits to care providers through preventive care, because catching issues faster means stopping them before they become life-altering, expensive problems to manage. For life sciences, it will help deepen understanding of disease to inform clinical development by using long-term patient histories to study progression and treatment outcomes, identify candidate biomarkers and find patients for clinical studies.

“We’re bringing general medical intelligence to [the] data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients,” added Lu.

#5345. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

If the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

#5344. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

#5341. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5339. AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates

Amazon Web Services Inc. is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major update to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.

Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a new family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.

AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.

After introducing Strands Harness, which allows Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment, in September, AWS followed up with Strands Decider one month later. Unlike regular LLMs that focus on text outputs, Strands Decider is a category of decision models designed to evaluate scenarios and assign probability scores to a predetermined list of choices. At the time, AWS said decision models can help to improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke to complete a given task.

With Strands Decider v2, AWS is adding five even more capable decision models to its lineup. The open-weight models are built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture and they’re available in various sizes, ranging from a lightweight edge version to a beefy 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. In a blog post, AWS explained that the new models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks, and deliver more optimal confidence scores, so agents can better determine when it’s OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker.

The Strands Decider v2 models have also been given the ability to process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents.

So far, AWS has used the Strands Decider v2 agents only internally, but it has seen impressive results. For instance, its engineers were able to replace Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on the company’s largest internal ticketing system, and in the process they were able to reduce its labelling costs by 98%.

They also cut ticket response times by 78%. But that’s not all they can do – in its experiments, AWS said, the new decider models showed an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models when a more computationally intensive frontier model might be overkill.

The Strands Decider v2 models are available to everyone now under an Apache 2.0 license and can be found on Hugging Face and also the Strands Decider repository on AWS.

Strands Decider is all about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. Meanwhile, Box CLI is all about securing them.

In a second blog post, AWS explained that many developers have taken to running their coding agents in what’s known as “YOLO mode.” That’s where they disable permission and configuration prompts so that those agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools as they see fit in order to complete a task. It’s named after the slang phrase “you only live once.”

Agents running in YOLO mode execute much faster, but they do so at the sacrifice of human oversight. And that’s dangerous. An agent without any restrictions can accidentally delete files it really shouldn’t or leak sensitive keys, or it can be manipulated through a malicious prompt to do something else that’s extremely damaging.

AWS’ solution to this is Strands Box, which is an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action. It launched last month, and with today’s update, it’s getting a new Box CLI that adds support for coding agents including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and the company’s very own Kiro CLI.

The idea is that developers can wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox to prevent any accidents from occurring. Within the sandbox, the agents will be able to work without restrictions, meaning they won’t have to keep pausing to ask a human developer for permission to do something important.

Instead, the developer simply applies security policies to safeguard the agent’s actions. These policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access, AWS explained.

The agent’s credentials live outside the sandbox, with application programming interface keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment. That way, the agent itself never has access to those sensitive keys.

AWS said developers also have the flexibility to switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access.

Like the new decider models, Box CLI in Strands Box is being launched today. It’s a big step forward for autonomous agents, ensuring they can work without constant interruptions while remaining on a very short leash.

#5338. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

#5336. Hyperliquid Anthropic Volume Explodes Past $1.7B as Hong Kong Issues Warning

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hyperliquid’s Anthropic market has surged to $1.7 billion in daily trading volume, pushing the contract ahead of Ethereum on the platform. The surge comes just as Hong Kong’s financial regulator adds Hyperliquid to its suspicious virtual asset trading platform list.

The ANT perpetual contract recorded $1.727 billion in trading volume over 24 hours on November 20. This has placed it second among Hyperliquid’s perpetual markets, behind Bitcoin but ahead of Ethereum.

Open interest also climbed to $259 million as traders built substantial positions rather than simply passing through short-term trades. The figures put Hyperliquid’s Anthropic market among the exchange’s most active markets, despite tracking a company outside the traditional crypto sector.

Just a day earlier, Anthropic ranked 17th among Hyperliquid perpetual contracts by trading volume. It then climbed to second place as activity accelerated around Anthropic’s public market debut. Its $1.727 billion turnover was 1.88 times Ethereum’s trading volume during the same period. Only Bitcoin attracted more activity, recording $5.139 billion.

The shift also displays how much Hyperliquid’s trading activity now extends beyond crypto-native assets. Six of the exchange’s top ten perpetual markets by volume were linked to traditional financial assets.

These included Anthropic, the XYZ100 technology index, the S&P 500, Nvidia, a leveraged semiconductor ETF, and South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix. Together, those six contracts generated $4.269 billion in volume, accounting for 38.1% of the top ten’s combined turnover.

ANT’s market has also attracted significant leverage. The contract allows traders to speculate on Anthropic’s share price using crypto collateral, without purchasing or owning the underlying shares.

Unlike conventional stock markets, the perpetual contract continues trading around the clock. This gives traders a venue to react to developments outside Nasdaq’s regular trading hours. This flexibility has helped attract activity as traders position themselves around major developments affecting the artificial intelligence sector.

Hyperliquid has demonstrated how much demand exists for trading assets beyond traditional crypto. Bitcoin Hyper is chasing a different opportunity: bringing Bitcoin liquidity into a much larger decentralized finance ecosystem.

The project is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) technology. Its goal is to let BTC holders move beyond simply holding their coins, opening access to faster transactions, decentralized exchanges, staking, and other DeFi applications.

That ambition is attracting considerable presale interest. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.29 million, with its token currently priced at just $0.01368760. More than 114,000 participants have joined the presale, giving the project considerable early fundraising momentum.

Staking is another major attraction, with the project offering rewards of up to 35% APY. That gives early participants an additional incentive to accumulate HYPER before its exchange debut, although actual rewards depend on the staking terms and participation.

Time is also becoming a factor. Bitcoin Hyper has scheduled its presale conclusion for November 26, putting its anticipated launch just days away. With the token still available below two cents, the approaching deadline could intensify demand among investors looking to secure an early position.

The trading surge comes against a growing regulatory problem for Hyperliquid. Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission added Hyperliquid and Hyperliquid Hong Kong to its suspicious virtual asset trading platforms list. The regulator specifically identified the platform’s trading interface at app.hyperliquid.xyz, stating that the entity was not licensed by the SFC.

The watchdog suspects the platform of operating, holding itself out as operating, or actively marketing an unlicensed virtual asset trading platform to the Hong Kong public.

The warning puts Hyperliquid under scrutiny in one of Asia’s most important financial centers. Hong Kong has spent recent years developing a licensing framework for crypto exchanges, requiring platforms serving local investors to obtain regulatory authorization.

The SFC also warned that investors using unlicensed platforms could lose their entire investment if an operator collapses, suffers a hack, or misappropriates customer assets.

#5335. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5334. At Arcadia University in Pennsylvania, Undergraduate Education Programs Are Plentiful

Arcadia's School of Education offers a variety of undergraduate education programs, including in-person, online, accelerated, and flexible pathways for students to get their degree and teaching certification.

GLENSIDE, Pa., Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Arcadia University, a top-ranked, private university in Greater Philadelphia with a long history of graduating teachers with high career outcomes, is proud to offer multiple pathways for individuals to earn a bachelor's degree in Education and become a teacher.

Most undergraduate Education majors at Arcadia earn a Bachelor of Arts (BA) in PreK-4 Education through the full-time, in-person program. Arcadia also offers:

"The need for highly skilled, compassionate, and innovative educators has never been greater," said Dr. Peggy Hickman, chair of the School of Education. "As schools face a critical teacher shortage, Arcadia University is committed to preparing the next generation of teachers to meet this challenge and make a lasting impact on students, schools, and communities."

Roughly half of Pennsylvania's local education agencies reported vacancies in the 2024-25 school year totaling more than 3,300, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Education. Moreover, high attrition rates (up to 9% for teachers with five or fewer years of experience) further demonstrate the dire need for new teachers.

Arcadia's strong partnerships with local schools and organizations, including the Philadelphia School District, mean students have a variety of fieldwork and student teaching opportunities; these experiences often lead to full-time employment post-graduation. A full 100 percent of School of Education graduates from the undergraduate Class of 2025 were employed or continuing their education within nine months of graduating.1 Arcadia Education alumni in the Philadelphia School District and beyond are also recipients of several prestigious education awards, including the Lindback Award for Distinguished Teaching, the Lindback Award for Principal Leadership, and the Presidential Award for Excellence in Mathematics and Science Teaching.

"What sets Arcadia University apart is its commitment, in partnership with Lindley Academy Charter School, to preparing teachers who fully understand and embrace the realities and rewards of education in the city," said Dr. Margery Covello, CEO of Lindley Academy Charter School in Philadelphia, which employs Arcadia Education students and graduates. "We are grateful for this partnership and proud that it has brought exceptional Arcadia University graduates onto our faculty."

To learn more about Arcadia's School of Education programs for undergraduate as well as graduate studies, visit arcadia.edu/school-of-education.

#5333. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”
