#5272. With Jensen Huang back as CEO, Nvidia’s SEC probe puts CFO Colette Kress in the spotlight

Following Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, Colette Kress is no longer interim CEO. But as finance chief, a lingering Securities and Exchange Commission investigation could put Kress under scrutiny, raising questions about her future at the AI giant.

The Fortune 500 company announced Monday that Huang had been reinstated as president and chief executive officer and as a member of the board, effective immediately. He had stepped down on Nov. 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman some officials believed was a Chinese spy. The White House told Fortune that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang getting reinstated, and Trump said the U.S. government did not believe Huang’s return posed any national security risk.

“We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s chief financial officer,” the company announcement said.

While the announcement indicated a return to Nvidia’s previous management structure, with Kress back in the finance chief role she’s held for the past 13 years, that may not be as easy as it appears. For one thing, it’s unclear whether the relationship between Kress and Huang has been damaged by the events of the past two weeks. And with Nvidia facing various investigations, Kress could be in the line of fire, depending on the outcome of the probes.

The SEC is investigating Nvidia’s accounting practices, Reuters reported last week. The Wall Street Journal previously reported the investigation, although its precise focus remains unclear. Nvidia didn’t respond to Fortune’s request for comment. An SEC spokesperson said the agency does not comment on “the existence or nonexistence of a possible investigation.”

An investigation does not necessarily mean wrongdoing has occurred. But the scrutiny could put Nvidia’s financial practices and corporate governance under a brighter spotlight, raising questions about what Kress knew about the company’s financial risks and when.

Kathryn Harrigan, a professor at Columbia Business School, pointed to Kress reportedly raising concerns internally last spring about Nvidia’s financial backing of loans to AI startups buying its chips. Kress questioned how borrowers were selected and how guarantees were valued, according to reports.

Nvidia has helped AI startups secure financing to buy its chips, creating a circular flow of money: The company supports buyers financially, and those buyers spend the money on Nvidia products. That makes it harder to assess underlying demand for its chips without that support, Harrigan said.

“In my book, Ms. Kress is a person who’s aware of the problem, and good luck to her if it’s an SEC investigation,” said Harrigan, a corporate strategy specialist. “When I served on boards, I’ve gone through that, and it’s just endless depositions, and they never tell you whether they’re satisfied or not.”

Harrigan added that Huang “had better brush up on whatever he told Ms. Kress back in the spring when they reportedly started to have a disagreement between them about how they were proceeding.”

During Nvidia’s Nov. 17 earnings call, Kress also signaled caution about financial commitments.

“We are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees,” she said, adding that Nvidia would be “disciplined and selective in our support.”

The way that Nvidia accounted for sales in Singapore has also come under scrutiny. Singapore was one of the company’s five geographic revenue locations until mid-2025, when Nvidia abruptly changed how it recorded revenue and removed Singapore from the list of locations. Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer suspected of evading U.S. chip export controls and the company at which Huang’s paramour was an executive, is based in Singapore.

Shawn Cole, president and cofounder of Cowen Partners Executive Search, said an SEC investigation involving financial oversight generally falls within the CFO’s purview.

“Nvidia’s potential exposure to securities class action litigation, compounded by alleged gaps in its directors and officers liability insurance, raises serious questions about corporate governance, financial oversight, and risk management,” Cole said.

Kress could face scrutiny over what she knew about these exposures, when she knew it, and her role in evaluating, disclosing, and mitigating those risks, he said.

Huang could also potentially have exposure for all of the same issues, of course. But as evidenced by Trump’s intervention in the board’s deliberations, the CEO has an important ally in his corner that Kress may not have.

Research suggests CFOs can face career consequences even when they are not implicated in corporate fraud. In “Fraud Firms’ Non-Implicated CFOs,” published in Contemporary Accounting Research, the authors found that roughly one-third of CFOs in its sample were not implicated in the misconduct, yet these executives experienced higher turnover and poorer subsequent employment prospects than peers at comparable companies—evidence that reputational damage can extend beyond those accused of wrongdoing.

When Nvidia announced Kress’s interim CEO appointment on Nov. 12, she said she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.” At the end of the Nov. 17 earnings call, she added: “Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed; we’ve got this.”

Kress had not publicly expressed interest in pursuing the permanent CEO position. The board had said it would consider internal and external candidates, but Huang’s reinstatement effectively ended that search.

CFOs are increasingly being appointed CEOs, and Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, played an extensive role in the company’s growth, and has vast finance experience at Cisco, Microsoft, and Texas Instruments.

“I’m not sure Kress wants to be CEO, but it is unlikely she will eventually be CEO of Nvidia,” Cole said. “Her short stint as interim CEO wasn’t long enough to impress.”

If Kress decides on her own to leave Nvidia, Cole said, her next step would most likely be retirement.

“I usually try to steer my students by reminding them that if they take a CFO job, that assumes that they know everything about the finances of the company and how the money gets made,” Harrigan said.

Sheryl Estrada is a senior writer at Fortune, where she covers the corporate finance industry, Wall Street, and corporate leadership. She also authors CFO Daily.

#5271. 4 lessons from Nvidia's board reversal on Jensen Huang's return

Nvidia's board reversed course on Jensen Huang within days. Four lessons show where that cost the board, its interim CEO and its credibility.

Boards exist to hold chief executives to account, and their final check is the power to remove one. That check works only if someone else can run the company once the chief executive is gone. When investors, employees and the public see a founder as the company itself, nobody can be sure that anyone else can. Jensen Huang left Nvidia $NVDA and was brought back by its board after an absence of 11 days, according to The Robot Report. That was too short a time to show whether Nvidia could manage without him. The episode is less a story about one chief executive than about how far a board's authority reaches once a founder's standing exceeds the board's own.

Investors made their view clear as soon as Huang left. They sharply cut Nvidia's market value after his departure, according to The Robot Report. The drop put the board at odds with the shareholders it answers to, and the costs of that mismatch spread well beyond the boardroom.

Fast Company drew out the governance lessons boards can take from Nvidia's brief leadership upheaval. They range from the thankless position of the executive who stands in for a departed founder to the gap between a board's credibility and its company's stock price. In each case, Nvidia's board made a decision it lacked the standing to hold. Huang got his job back, but the board came out of the reversal with less authority than it had going in.

A statement on an earnings call becomes a board's promise to every investor at once. Nvidia $NVDA Board Chair Harvey Jones used that setting to rule out Huang's return, then reversed himself within days, according to Fast Company. The Robot Report reports that Jones spoke on the Nov. 17 call and that the board voted to reinstate Huang six days later. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Jones said. The board had gone back on its own word, and investors now have reason to doubt the next thing it rules out.

Jones made his promise while the pressure against it was already public, and that pressure kept up until the board gave in. President Donald Trump voiced support for Huang's possible return on Nov. 16, the day before the earnings call, and again on Nov. 22, the day before the board voted, according to The Robot Report. Support for Huang also reached well beyond Washington, as backers put more than 200,000 signatures on a "Stand With Jensen" petition, according to . Nothing on record shows which of these pressures changed the directors' minds, but the board staked its word against a campaign that was already under way.

A board's oversight of a chief executive rests on one implied threat: if the CEO fails, someone else can do the job. Boards lose that ordinary power once a founder seems too vital to replace, according to Fast Company, and Nvidia $NVDA met that condition. Duncan Clark, speaking on CNBC's "Access Middle East," judges that no single person could take over Huang's role. Nvidia's directors had the least leverage at the moment the founder mattered most, which is exactly when they would most want to use it.

Nvidia $NVDA's shareholders and its critics reached opposite verdicts about the same week. Critics see the episode as a governance failure while shareholders celebrate the stock's rally, according to Fast Company. Nvidia shares were up more than 30% before the market opened Monday, after the board reversed course and reinstated Huang, according to ABC News. Shareholders were celebrating the founder's return, not the judgment of the directors who had tried to do without him.

Shareholders celebrated before anyone had answered the questions behind the upheaval. The SEC and the Department of Justice are continuing their investigations, ABC News , and the board's own committee investigation is set to proceed to its conclusion. The directors brought Huang back before their own inquiry had finished. Shareholders now hold stock whose value depends on findings nobody has seen yet, and nothing in Monday's gains protects them if those findings go badly.

Not one director held to the chair's position when the vote came. The Robot Report reports that the decision to bring Huang back was unanimous. A unanimous reversal in less than a week leaves two explanations, and neither reflects well on the directors. Either the board never fully supported the original position, or the pressure left no director willing to defend it.

Any board can leave itself room to change course, because "not now" can survive pressure that "never" cannot.

At Nvidia, the board's check on its founder had barely been built. The company had no board chair at all before Jones, according to CNBC, and Clark calls the situation a governance failure. The founder did not overpower a board that had been working. The board had never been set up to oversee him in the first place, and the crisis brought that weakness into public view.

A founder's fame calls for more board independence, not less, in the view of Linda Ford $F, chief executive of The Chartered Governance Institute in the U.K. "A high-profile leader can be an asset, but the board needs to work hard to protect its independence and provide the scrutiny shareholders are entitled to expect," Ford told CNBC. Nvidia's board now has to build that independence after its founder has already shown he outranks the directors, which is the hardest point at which to start.

Huang won this round, and Nvidia has yet to show that a new chair can give real scrutiny to a founder back in command.

Nvidia $NVDA's stand-in chief kept the company steady while speaking for a decision the board would not keep. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress led Nvidia through the turmoil and then smoothly returned control to Huang, according to Fast Company. She took the job after a long run as the company's finance chief, a post she has held since 2013, according to CNBC. As interim chief, she also gave the board's refusal her own voice in public. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen," Kress said. She then handed the company back by carrying out the opposite of what she had told the public, and that gap is the thankless part of the job.

The board's refusal had to hold up inside Nvidia, too. A petition urging Huang's return drew more than 10,000 signers who described themselves as Nvidia employees, out of a workforce of roughly 42,000, according to CNBC. Kress assured the public that employees were committed, yet a sizable part of the staff she was meant to lead had put their names behind Huang. At an internal meeting, Kress changed the subject when Huang came up.

When the board reversed its position, the executive who had voiced it was the one left exposed, not the directors who set it. With control back in Huang's hands, Kress works for the man whose return she ruled out in public.

A board that makes its stand-in the public voice of a stance it cannot guarantee is spending that executive's credibility, not its own.

The board will have to rebuild its credibility in Washington, where a share price carries no weight. Doubt about the board's assurance that Huang poses no security risk reaches into the Republican Party. "No national security risk? Based on what?" Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn said, as ABC News reported. Democrats bring institutional power to that scrutiny, since Sen. Elizabeth Warren is the incoming chair of the Banking Committee. Lawmakers with that kind of authority can keep asking their questions long after the news cycle moves on.

Shareholders got their founder back. The directors still have to win back the trust of regulators and Congress, and no gain in the stock can do that for them.

#5270. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5268. U.S. filed forfeiture complaint to recover more than $1 billion from Binance hack

Prosecutors allege some of the money sits at identified crypto addresses after a hack that took about $6.3 billion

The U.S. Justice Department lodged a complaint in Washington's federal court on Monday asking to forfeit over $1 billion in crypto that hackers tied to North Korea took from Binance Holdings, according to Bloomberg.

According to Bloomberg, investigators and prosecutors traced some of the money to specific virtual currency addresses, where they allege it was held after the attack. The attack netted roughly $6.3 billion, one of the biggest hacks ever recorded.

"Today's action underscores the critical role of public-private partnerships in combating cryptocurrency-enabled crime," Tysen Duva, head of the Justice Department's criminal division, said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. "By working closely with the digital asset industry, we can disrupt illicit financial activity, protect victims, and recover stolen assets before they move beyond the reach of law enforcement."

Binance publicly confirmed the intrusion and blamed North Korea for it. The company said the breach was a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that put malicious software on the laptop of one of its engineers, according to Bloomberg. Someone claiming to hold the role of project director had approached the engineer on a website for job seekers.

A Binance spokesperson said in a statement, according to Bloomberg: "We are coordinating closely with the DOJ as well as all of our industry partners that have assisted in freezing assets impacted by the hack. We expect to continue to cooperate with DOJ throughout the asset forfeiture process with the goal of securing the return of those funds as expediently as possible."

Earlier this month, the Justice Department obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency. The department attributed the theft to members of the North Korean military, whom the FBI calls "TraderTraitor," and said they stole more than $6 billion in virtual assets on or about Oct. 29. Government and private-sector efforts had frozen more than $2.7 billion, the department said, and the $1.2 billion was part of that total.

The department said at the time that efforts to trace, freeze, seize and forfeit the assets were ongoing. It said TraderTraitor actors continued to launder the funds through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges.

Binance has since made customers whole for the entire $6.3 billion taken in the hack, the exchange said. North Korea has denied the claim that it was responsible.

#5267. AI startups feared Nvidia’s money would dry up without Jensen Huang. His return as CEO has put those fears to rest

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after just shy of two weeks of turmoil. The news—which has come as a shock to many in the tech world—was a welcome relief to investors and Nvidia’s partners, who had spent the majority of that time fretting that the company’s financial commitments might dry up.

Nvidia has become what some have referred to as the “central bank of AI.” The company has invested in and supplied compute to various AI startups, neoclouds, and AI labs. These companies then, in part, use that money to buy Nvidia chips. Critics have called this process “circular financing,” with many saying it leaves much of the AI boom dangerously exposed to weak links.

Indeed as of the end of July, Nvidia had invested nearly $50 billion in AI model makers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, and its equity stakes across the AI ecosystem totaled twice that. It has also pledged $170 billion of its investment-grade credit to help AI companies and neoclouds get financing.

Before news of Huang’s reinstatement broke on Monday, several investors and Nvidia partners told Fortune they were concerned that these commitments might stall under the interim CEO. That interim CEO, Colette Kress, some said, already showed early signs of being more hesitant to make deals at the same rate as Huang. Any new CEO, they added, would likely want to appear as a steady hand and more cautious when it came to spending.

“Jensen has been such a critical part of the ecosystem because he’s allowed Nvidia to provide compute to venture stage companies who otherwise don’t have access to it,” said one investor who asked to be anonymous to discuss private deals. “Everyone was concerned about whether the next person at the helm of Nvidia would also be as aggressive in fostering that ecosystem.”

For a while, the investor said, any startup that landed a meeting with Huang was likely to walk away with funding.

There were also worries about commitments to so-called neoclouds, such as CoreWeave or Nscale. These companies buy Nvidia GPUs, often with large amounts of debt, and rent the computing power to AI labs, startups, and enterprises. Nvidia has taken equity stakes in some of them and guarantees some of their data center leases. It has also agreed to rent back unused capacity at a fixed rate, which gives banks a floor that makes them more willing to lend. For example, Nvidia has agreed to buy up to $6.3 billion of CoreWeave’s unsold capacity through 2032.

If Nvidia pulled back on some of these investments, the neoclouds most exposed would be those selling capacity to buyers without investment-grade credit, since they might not be able to finance GPUs without a backstop. This could have the knock-on effect of slowing some new data center projects.

Huang’s personal touch extended to Nvidia’s supply chain, too. After his resignation, Elon Musk wrote on X that many of Nvidia’s critical deals were “a handshake with Jensen” and warned that “at least some of those critical deals will be lost” without him.

With Huang back at the helm, investors expect Nvidia to keep acting as the AI industry’s lender; AI startups, labs, and neoclouds that lean on Nvidia for funding, compute, and credit backstops have more reason to expect those deals will keep coming at the pace they’d grown used to. The market seemed to agree, with Nvidia shares jumping more than 30% on Monday, and analysts at Melius Research and Bernstein quickly upgrading the stock.

“Jensen Huang’s return is an enormous positive for Nvidia and the broader AI trade, removing a major source of uncertainty and restoring the visionary leadership that helped build the entire AI infrastructure ecosystem,” said David Miller, CIO at Catalyst Funds. “While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today’s announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector.”

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. Asset manager Bitwise has filed an S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a spot Zcash (ZEC) exchange-traded fund. The document appeared in the SEC's database on Nov. 17, 2026. On Wednesday, ZEC rose to $975 before it pulled back to around $927.

Zcash is often called a "more secret" version of Bitcoin. According to the S-1, the Zcash network supports two types of transactions, and the "shielded" ones use a form of zero-knowledge cryptography known as zk-SNARKs. Holders of shielded Zcash "may selectively disclose transaction information to third parties," the filing says.

Bitwise's fund will not use this feature. "The Trust does not engage in shielded transactions in connection with its activities," according to the document.

The shares are expected to list on the Dallas-based Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) under the ticker ZEC. According to the S-1, Coinbase Custody Trust Company will act as the Zcash custodian, and BNY Mellon will serve as the cash custodian. Bitwise also wrote that "the Trust will not stake or otherwise seek to derive additional Zcash from its holdings." The sponsor fee in the filing is listed as "0.___% per annum."

In the risk section of the S-1, Bitwise wrote that "a number of digital asset trading platforms have delisted Zcash, restricted trading in Zcash or declined to support Zcash." According to the filing, many of these platforms cited regulatory or compliance concerns.

The platforms that still support Zcash "do so only with respect to transparent addresses and do not permit deposits or withdrawals to or from shielded addresses," the document says. Bitwise also pointed to new EU rules that take effect on July 10, 2027. According to the S-1, the rules will "prohibit credit institutions, financial institutions and crypto-asset service providers in the European Union" from keeping accounts in such assets.

Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan named Zcash one of his top three assets for the decade in September, alongside Bitcoin and tokenization projects. Three days before the S-1 filing, he called ZEC a "golden mean" between open Bitcoin and anonymous Monero in an interview.

Grayscale's Zcash fund (ZCSH) has traded on NYSE Arca since August 2026, and the Winklevoss brothers filed for their own Zcash ETF on Nasdaq in October. ZCSH held $496.79 million as of the Nov. 17 close, according to SoSoValue. The fund has attracted $168.76 million in net inflows since its launch, and it recorded no inflows on Nov. 17, when Bitwise filed its S-1.

#5265. Jensen Huang’s return is what Silicon Valley wanted—but things won’t necessarily be the same

Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy led to his ouster from Nvidia. Eleven days later, he’s back—the outcome Silicon Valley founders, watchers, and luminaries wanted all along.

Within hours of Huang’s original (and ignominious) exit from Nvidia earlier this month, a “Stand With Jensen” petition circulated online, demanding Huang’s return to the company he’d cofounded in 1993. Signatories included Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Atreides Management CIO Gavin Baker, and Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi, who wrote in the comments, “Nvidia runs on Jensen! Bring him back!”

Travis Kalanick, Uber’s pugnacious cofounder and former CEO, was both a signatory and especially vocal in his support.

“Jensen is one of the great builders of our time,” Kalanick—himself ousted in 2017 from Uber amid compounding scandals—wrote in a public post on the “Stand With Jensen” site. “Liberty and civilizational progress depend on Jensen,” Kalanick declared. “He has erred, yes—to err is to be human—but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company. Jensen deserves fairness in adjudication and we must presume innocence until that adjudication proves otherwise beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Huang’s return is a Rorschach test of sorts. Some critics see a corporate governance nightmare, while much of the wider public has memed or expressed horror at the circumstances of Huang’s initial resignation (widely described as potentially raising national security concerns). In Silicon Valley though, Huang’s ouster was an injustice that trumped any other aspects of the story. To tech, Huang remains the most indispensable of founders, a nearly godlike figure in a culture that worships “founder mode.”

So, Huang’s return, however questionable it may be, is cause for celebration. Even the very circumspect Sam Altman, who’d previously expressed cautious sympathy for Huang (and who of course, went through a very similar ordeal), tweeted on X on Monday, “Jensen!” Musk, meanwhile, tweeted: “The mistake has been corrected.” Sarah Guo, the plugged-in founder of Conviction VC, welcomed Huang back. The chorus from tech was, in its way, relatively unanimous about just how positive this news was. (The markets agreed vigorously; Nvidia closed today up about 31%, after last week’s massive tech rout.) Meanwhile, for Nvidia’s board, it’s a dicey U-turn.

“Six days after Nvidia’s board said it had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, he’s back—before the board’s own independent investigation has reported anything, before he answers questions from Congress next week, and with no conditions attached (or at least none that anyone outside the boardroom can see),” said Nicole Bestard, founder of communications firm Quarter Horse Strategies, via email. “From a reputation standpoint, this is a huge mistake. It asks investors, employees, and the public to take the board’s judgment on faith.”

The move from here, in part, is likely to attempt to bury this, David Tepper, cofounder and CEO of Ascerta, predicts.

“It very likely means that Nvidia will be putting out their next GPU cycle (the 6000 series) much sooner than otherwise expected,” he said via email. “They will be eager to bury the news cycle with Nvidia’s continued dominance in the space versus keeping the attention on his infidelity.”

Nevertheless, things are not likely to be the same from here on out, said Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

“No one can replace the vision he has,” said Padval. “With him back, he may not go back to 100% immediately, he’ll likely be more cautious. It will still be significantly better than a few weeks back.”

Translation: We still can’t assume Huang will continue to be as aggressive an investor, operator, and guarantor as he may have been before, even with a supposed return to normalcy.

“The private markets ecosystem has to stand by itself,” said Padval. “This was driven by Nvidia a lot in the past, the whole AI ecosystem. If participation is less, the venture community needs to step it up with conviction. We all need to believe in the companies we’re backing. And if we believe in the companies, [we] don’t have to wait for the signal from Nvidia.”

Allie Garfinkle is a senior writer and editor at Fortune, where she runs Term Sheet; leads coverage of private capital, investors, and startups; and co-chairs the Brainstorm conference series.

#5264. Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. Here's why

Figures like Huang, like Steve Jobs, come as a single package. We can't call on their genius without also living with their limits

Jensen Huang is back. One reading of why: He won the power struggle because he sat at the center of an ecosystem of buyers, suppliers, and financiers, all of whom depended on his word, his skill, and his vision.

Nvidia $NVDA doesn't just sell into the AI build-out. It finances it, and in doing it has taken on risks that could ripple well beyond the company. The AI chipmaker has invested $30 billion in OpenAI, which buys computing power from Nvidia's customers. It put $2 billion into CoreWeave, a customer that rents Nvidia-powered computing to AI developers. It agreed to buy CoreWeave's unsold capacity through 2032, a backstop initially valued at $6.3 billion. It gives some large customers 3-12 months to pay. It committed up to $10 billion to Anthropic, which in turn committed to buy $30 billion of computing from Microsoft $MSFT's Azure, which runs partly on Nvidia systems. Nvidia's money funds Anthropic, which pays

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

Nvidia also lends out its credit standing. It has taken on up to $118 billion in guarantees that lenders and landlords rely on, including up to $105 billion backing OpenAI's leases at SB Energy's Ohio data-center campus. And it is working with Blackstone, Apollo, KKR and others to raise more than $500 billion of outside capital, on which it may cover up to a quarter of a project's residual value.

This circular financing is risky. If demand for computing power falls behind supply, Nvidia would absorb losses as seller, investor, backstop buyer, and guarantor all at once. Its share price would fall sharply, dragging down the market and tightening credit elsewhere in the economy.

Nvidia's counterparties saw Huang as the personal guarantor of this fragile system. In March, speaking of TSMC $TSM, Huang said: "I don't know how many tens, hundreds of billions of dollars of business we've done through them, and we don't have a contract." Suppliers invest upstream, he added, "because I said to the CEOs, 'Let me tell you how big this industry is going to be.'"

Two days after Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following revelations of multiple affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, Elon Musk said on social media that "many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract."

Finance, I'd argue, is 10% math and 90% psychology.

Here's a more Machiavellian reading of what happened Monday when Nvidia's board reinstated Huang less than two weeks after his ouster: Huang planned his resignation as a springboard back. Think game theory. Had he stayed, every new revelation would have weakened him further. By resigning first, he took the sting out of whatever came next, since he'd already fessed up. And he let everyone feel what life without him looked like.

Nvidia's stock was hammered in the days before and after his departure, and all three major market indexes ended last week in correction territory as the wider market slumped with Nvidia. Partners worried his handshake deals would fall apart. Within days, an unnamed ally told the Financial Times they were assembling a "war room" to lobby for his return.

The board chair said during the company's earnings call last week that Huang wasn't coming back. Six days later, he was back. Nvidia stock quickly soared 35%. The rest of the market followed.

The board's statement is revealing. It outsourced its judgment to Washington, saying that "senior levels of the United States government" had assured it Huang posed no national security risk. Trump later called his own intervention "very important." To him, Huang was an ace in the hole in the AI race with China. The board, which had cited Huang's lack of candor, now declared itself "satisfied" with it.

That was a climbdown. Nvidia reinstated him before its own investigation had concluded. Huang offered humility and thanks to his family, but no fresh apology upon his return. The board also announced a search for a chief compliance officer, reporting to a board committee. Whoever takes the job will be a watchdog for the board while depending on Huang's cooperation. Don't envy them. Score it Huang 2, Board 1.

Huang is larger than life. Few doubt his genius, even as many recoil at his disregard for protocol. We talk about economic forces, but they are embodied in the people who make decisions and take risks on our behalf. Almost 200,000 people signed a petition for his return, more than 10,000 of whom said they were Nvidia employees.

Figures like Huang, like Steve Jobs, come as a single package. We can't call on their genius without also living with their limits. They live in the world of ideas rather than people, which is why they feel free to break rules and norms. Institutions exist to check them.

Larry Hirschhorn is a management consultant and expert on the psychodynamics of organizations.

#5263. XRP Ledger Scores Historic First in Global Banking Standards Review

XRP Ledger (XRPL) has marked a significant step in its journey to institutional adoption by becoming the first public permissionless layer-1 blockchain to see its principles of Architecture and Resiliency independently verified by the Global Layer One (GL1) Market Infrastructure Toolkit.

The foundation’s self-assessment was independently verified by the blockchain security firm CertiK on the responses and evidence submitted around the principles of Architecture and Resiliency.

The independent attestation report was released on Nov. 13, further strengthening the assertion of XRP Ledger's compliance with institutional financial infrastructure requirements.

This comes at a time when banks and asset managers are increasingly considering blockchain technology to enable tokenization of deposits, stablecoins, investment funds and other financial instruments.

The Global Layer One initiative is a collaborative effort between prominent financial institutions and policymakers to set standards for digital financial infrastructure.

Its main goal is to make cross-border transactions for tokenised assets seamless while ensuring that blockchain networks adhere to internationally expected standards for financial market infrastructure.

Interestingly, XRPLF self-assessed XRPL for all 10 principles.

CertiK independently verified it only for the principles of Architecture and Resiliency.

XRPLF also provided details on how requirements specific to private/permissioned networks are addressed by managing related risks for XRPL’s decentralized nature, open-source governance model, and protocol amendments.

XRP Ledger Foundation executive director Brett Mollin emphasized the need to give financial institutions tangible evidence instead of pitching ideas.

Mollin added that independent attestation from CertiK also gives financial institutions more confidence while vetting the network.

It does not mean that XRPL meets all the standards mentioned in the toolkit completely.

The XRP Ledger Foundation will continue to update its assessment in line with the development of GL1 principles and XRPL protocol amendments that are activated.

Nonetheless, it's another step towards XRPL's bid to be a possible infrastructure for regulated financial institutions looking for blockchain-based settlement and tokenization.

The Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) on Nov. 18 with seven recommendations on the draft documents CP26/36 and GC26/7. Three of them concern CP26/36, and four concern GC26/7. The letter was signed by HPC chief executive Jake Chervinsky.

The UK's new crypto regime will start to apply on Oct. 25, 2027. The FCA opened its window for crypto license applications on Sept. 30, 2026, and the window will close on Feb. 28, 2027.

According to the letter, "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity." HPC argued that attaching obligations to a person who could not discharge them "would offer consumers no additional protection."

In the letter, HPC also compared public blockchains with the internet. "Like a public blockchain, the internet depends on protocols that identifiable persons maintain and upgrade over time," the group wrote.

HPC asked the FCA to assess each participant in a blockchain network separately. Proprietary traders and market makers "supply much of the liquidity on which order books depend," the group wrote. HPC also asked the regulator to describe compliance requirements as outcomes and to hold regulated firms accountable for them.

On Aug. 24, HPC urged the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to harmonize their rules for perpetual contracts. The group argued that such products should be classified by their economic structure. According to HPC, a harmonized framework would let exchanges compete on "execution quality and liquidity."

On Sept. 30, HPC sent its response to the European Union's review of the MiCA rules. In it, the group asked the EU to treat crypto perpetual futures as derivatives under MiFID II. "Clarity in application, rather than new legislation, is what would assist in regulating perpetual futures," HPC wrote at the time.

Chervinsky previously served as chief policy officer at the Blockchain Association and as chief legal officer at the crypto venture firm Variant.

#5260. ‘Doesn’t answer the big questions’: The stock market is still $5 trillion below its AI-fueled peak despite Monday’s rally

Wall Street’s full-blown gamble on the AI boom helped wipe out $8 trillion in stock market value before Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia helped lead a rebound Monday.

Wall Street had its best day since April 2025 on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, 11 days after he resigned. The S&P 500 closed up about 5%, while the Nasdaq was up 6.5% and the Dow 3%, while Nvidia shares jumped 33%. Even so, the rally won back only about $3 trillion of the roughly $8 trillion the S&P 500 lost in the six weeks after its Oct. 6 record, leaving the index still about $5 trillion below its peak.

The swing shows how much of the stock market now rides on the AI trade. And Monday’s rally didn’t answer the question that started the selloff: whether the billions of dollars companies have poured into AI will pay off.

As of Friday’s close, the three biggest U.S. indexes had suffered steep losses with no relief in sight. The S&P 500, which tracks the broader market, was down 3.7%. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the Dow Jones industrial average fell 5.3% and 1.9%, respectively, with all three indexes wading into correction territory on Friday.

The AI-fueled collapse of the past few weeks came after the S&P 500 reached a fresh record high on Oct. 6, when the companies in the index were collectively worth roughly $70 trillion. By Friday, just six weeks later, that value had plummeted more than 11%, erasing roughly $8 trillion in value, before Monday’s rebound.

The losses highlight how dependent the broader stock market has become on the AI boom. Of the top 10 biggest U.S. companies, which make up 40% of the S&P 500, eight of them are tech companies. The concentration problem also extends globally. The U.S. now makes up three-quarters of the value of stocks in developed markets worldwide, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in a note Monday.

Trump told CNBC Monday he “convinced” the company’s board to reinstate Huang.

“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” he told the outlet.

White House communications director Steven Cheung confirmed to multiple outlets that Trump was “totally involved” in bringing Huang back as CEO. The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Setting aside questions about corporate governance and national security raised by some high profile politicians—including Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee—Monday’s rally gave the market a much-needed boost while at the same time highlighting other issues.

eToro market analyst Sam North told the Guardian that while Monday’s stock rebound highlights the concentration of the AI trade and its dependence on one man, Nvidia “restoring its founder to the helm gives investors a powerful reason to reassess last week’s selloff.”

Nvidia was among the hardest hit by the stock market slide in recent weeks. Shares of the AI chip giant fell nearly 14% Friday and 23% over the week, wiping out hundreds of billions of dollars in market value.

The plunge came despite stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings, with the company surpassing $100 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time. Still, concerns over AI spending and the company’s future prospects without Huang at the top rattled investors.

Memory-chip manufacturers also suffered alongside Nvidia. Micron Technology plunged nearly 24% for the week, while other chipmakers like AMD and Broadcom both saw their stocks fall by double digits.

Anthropic, meanwhile, had its blockbuster IPO overshadowed almost immediately by the selloff. The Claude maker raised more than $81 billion in its Thursday debut, the largest IPO in history, only to see its shares tumble 8.5% Friday. On Friday, Anthropic’s stock was trading flat for the day at about $89. By Monday, the stock had closed down another 1.4% to about $87 per share.

Last week’s pain also extended to data center operators like CoreWeave and Nebius, which also saw steep stock declines, after their shares had already fallen in the aftermath of the blue wave midterm election that raised concerns about newly elected Democrats imposing tougher restrictions on data center development.

While Huang’s return has restored some confidence in the AI trade, it has not resolved the industry’s bigger questions about the billions of dollars in spending companies have put into AI and whether they can justify their soaring valuations, said James St. Aubin, the chief investment officer of Ocean Park Asset Management.

“​The AI story was already facing pressure before the ​Jensen story broke. Jensen’s return doesn’t answer the ⁠big questions investors were grappling with regarding the ROI on the AI build-out,” he said.

#5259. Red Robin Is Selling 116 Restaurants to Franchisees — Here’s Why It’s Flying Against the Casual-Dining Flock

Nearly half its locations will soon be franchisee-owned, a rare move for a sit-down restaurant these days.

Red Robin Gourmet Burgers is shifting from restaurant operator to franchisor. The casual-dining chain sold 108 company-owned locations to franchisees for $89.4 million in September and has eight more sales in the works, according to Restaurant Business. Once those close, about 45% of its almost 450 restaurants will be franchisee-owned, up from 19% at the end of last year.

The sales are due to debt. CEO David Pace calls refranchising “a very tactical exercise to raise proceeds in order to pay down existing debt.” Red Robin cut its long-term debt 44% to $91.9 million and refinanced at a rate 400 basis points lower. The new owners pay the brand a 4.5% royalty.

More deals could follow. Pace says buyers are still interested, and Red Robin will consider offers if the partner, valuation and geography are right.

The strategy runs against the grain in sit-down dining. Chili’s, Texas Roadhouse and First Watch have been buying back franchised stores, and even Applebee’s has reacquired some. Red Robin’s hopes the new strategy works. Shares fell more than 23% after its latest earnings.

#5257. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5255. ‘Superintelligence is arriving’: Mark Zuckerberg’s AI chief warns humanity may lose control as the AI bubble refuses to pop

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs, posted on X on Sunday that “superintelligence is arriving.” He wrote that “the models are clearly going to be intelligent enough to automate all of AI research,” and that “it is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement.” He said the remaining obstacles are “no longer intelligence; they are domain-specific know-how, plumbing, and experimentation.”

“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang wrote.

Social media erupted over the latest warning from inside the AI thunderdome during a weekend when the AI bubble seemed to finally have popped—the day before it controversially reinflated again. Wang wasn’t even posting about Anthropic’s IPO or Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia—to be followed by his sudden reinstatement on Monday morning.

He was riffing on just the latest historic math breakthrough with the help of generative AI: the claim by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic’s technical staff, of a proof of the Riemann hypothesis made with Anthropic’s Claude. The 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s $1 million Millennium Prize problems.

“It is hard to overstate the magnitude of discovery that we have just witnessed,” Wang wrote about the milestone, describing it as completed “with the help of an alien mind that we don’t understand.” He added that building an atomic bomb is “a homework problem compared to the Riemann hypothesis.”

Wang’s warning came as Meta expects to devote $135 billion to $145 billion to capital expenditures this year, driven largely by AI infrastructure costs.

Wang’s post spread fast. The Next Web counted more than 8 million views in its first half day, and the reaction crossed the usual political lines. Jon Favreau, President Obama’s former director of speechwriting, called it “f—ing madness” and said the people Americans elected should be doing everything they can to stop the frontier labs “from handing over control of humanity to superintelligent machines.”

From the right, Megyn Kelly posted: “This is the head of Meta’s superintelligence lab. We’ve had similar warnings from Anthropic, the former head of alignment at OpenAI, not to mention Elon himself at X. How many more do we need until we garner the all-hands-on-deck reaction this deserves?”

Wang argued against fatalism. He wrote that he noticed “a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry”: the view that “ASI is inevitable and the only problem to solve is how to do it safely.” He added, “We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

After the backlash, he wrote, “What I am saying is, this path is not inevitable,” and “leaders and leadership matter more than ever.” He pointed to Meta’s decision to delay the launch of its Muse model for months and to Zuckerberg’s call for most computing power to go toward serving customers rather than toward AI that improves itself.

Zuckerberg made Wang the center of Meta’s AI push in June 2025, when Meta invested $14.3 billion in Wang’s former company, Scale AI, for a 49% stake. In January, Zuckerberg told investors that “this is going to be a big year for delivering personal superintelligence.” Meta has raised the bottom of its 2026 spending guidance at every quarterly report since, from $115 billion in January to $135 billion in October.

As for the Riemann hypothesis, Anthropic’s Alpöge has said he plans to explain the AI-generated proof in talks and a written account. Until mathematicians read it, the Clay Institute’s $1 million stays unclaimed.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5254. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

#5253. Gonka AI Hit by $1 Million Exploit as Hacker Drains Stablecoins

Decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) network Gonka AI has reportedly suffered a massive security attack in which hackers exploited its Ethereum bridge to withdraw stablecoins and issue unbacked tokens worth over $1 million.

According to blockchain analytics firm Onchain Lens, the hacker was able to gain access to the bridge's BLS group key, allowing the attacker to withdraw funds and issue Wrapped Gonka (WGNK) tokens without backing them with the required assets.

Per the report, the hacker managed to withdraw $884,800 in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) stablecoins and also issued $172,000 in unbacked WGNK tokens.

Combined, the total value of the affected assets stood at around $1.06 million, per Onchain Lens.

Following the hack, the funds were transferred through the decentralized exchange Uniswap and multiple crypto wallets, making it challenging to trace their final destination.

The attack targeted Gonka AI's cross-chain bridge. The cross-chain bridge makes it possible to transfer assets from Gonka AI's native chain to Ethereum and vice versa.

According to the project's technical documentation, withdrawing funds from Gonka to Ethereum requires certain cryptographic signatures from the network's validator set.

The cryptographic signatures are checked against the BLS group key, which changes with every network epoch.

Per the report, the attacker was able to change the epoch BLS group key on the bridge, making it possible for the hacker to control the part of the bridge responsible for authorizing fund withdrawals.

Thus, the hacker was able to withdraw funds from the bridge's stablecoin reserves and issue WGNK tokens without locking the required amount of assets on the native blockchain.

Blockchain security firm Blockaid noted that the hack had taken place, with the total amount of funds stolen reaching about $1.05 million across roughly five transactions at the time of the initial alert.

At the time it spotted the suspicious activity, Blockaid noted that the hack was still ongoing.

Onchain Lens's numbers differ slightly, with the firm reporting around $884,800 in stablecoin withdrawals and $172,000 in unbacked WGNK issuance.

Notably, the issuance of unbacked tokens presents an additional problem, given that such tokens could potentially enter circulation without the necessary reserves to back them.

#5251. The Best Publicity Isn’t a Headline. Here’s What Built My Business Instead.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I get a lot of LinkedIn requests, but I don’t connect for the sake of connecting. A thoughtful note and a 15-minute call have done more for my business than any press hit.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas. I’ve put founders on morning shows and turned product launches like IQBAR and Molecule Sleep into headlines. The work I love most, though, happens before any marketing campaign or pitch goes out: sitting with a founder and figuring out what they actually stand for. I know how reputations get built.

Almost all of my business has always come from referrals. In 2020, I started treating myself more like a client and following the advice I always give: build relationships before you need them, with people who’ll gladly vouch for you. I gave more talks, presented on webinars, spoke on conference panels and launched my newsletter. My favorite was a webinar I gave for MBA and EMBA students through BlueSteps called “LinkedIn Tips for Personal Branding.”

It’s paid off, and it started with being more selective and intentional.

If you’re connected to me on LinkedIn, we’ve talked. That’s on purpose. I get a lot of requests, but I don’t connect just to connect.

My filter is simple: a thoughtful note, or a profile that makes me curious. When someone clears that bar, I message them, introduce myself and suggest a 15-minute intro call by phone or Zoom. You can call me while you’re commuting, cooking dinner or taking a walk. I like to get to know the person first, then the business.

LinkedIn Premium is what makes this work for me. Seeing who’s viewed my profile tells me who’s already curious, and messaging lets me reach people with a personal note instead of a cold request. It’s what I’ve always done at conferences and events: walk across the room, say hello and ask how someone’s really doing.

A couple of years ago, I reached out to someone this way. We had two phone calls. No pitch, no deck, just getting to know each other.

After that second call, he referred me to two prospective clients. When I spoke with them, they told me something I’ll never forget: “If Michael trusts you, then we trust you.”

That sentence is the whole lesson. In PR, we talk about earned media versus paid media. Relationships work the same way. Trust that someone else earned with you and passed along is the most powerful credential you’ll ever have, and no ad can buy it.

A network you actually know pays off in another way: it’s the best search engine I have. When I need a partner or a service, I go to my network first. “Does anyone have a stellar digital growth performance agency?” gets me answers from people whose judgment I already trust, which beats a page of search results every time.

Being picky pays off here, too. Over the years, the people I know well have become my own personal advisory board.

The other half of building my own presence has been content. I publish a newsletter on LinkedIn called Spreading Sunshine. It’s personal by design. I share the latest in health and wellness, including my own protocols, along with business tips and a little joy. Readers tell me it feels like a note from a friend, which is exactly the point.

People now reach out because of what I post. The content does the introducing for me. By the time we get on that 15-minute call, they already know what I care about, and the conversation starts three steps ahead.

A personal profile and a company page do different jobs, and founders need both. SMACK! Media has its own page. When I launched Anything Brands, an all-natural skin remedy balm inspired by my own family, we set up a page for it, too.

My team uses the company pages for press hits, milestones and education. My personal page is where relationships happen; the company page is where credibility lives. When a retailer, a partner or a reporter looks us up, they find a consistent story in both places, and a founder they can actually reach.

Treat your network like your most important client. Be selective. Be generous. Show up as a human.

Ready to put that into practice? LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make those 15-minute conversations easier to start.

My favorite part is still the people: hearing about a founder’s big win, how someone got through a tough quarter, their kids, their dogs, how they juggle it all. If one of those calls leaves someone a little less burned out, that’s part of what fuels my positivity and boundless energy.

Some of my best relationships started with someone on the other end of the line, a little out of breath from a walk or with dinner sizzling in the background. Those calls rarely feel like business. After 30 years, I’ve learned the best publicity isn’t a headline. It’s someone who knows you saying your name in a room you’re not in. That’s exactly what Michael did for me. Treating myself like a client has been the best campaign I’ve ever run.

For 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas. I’ve put founders on morning shows and turned product launches like IQBAR and Molecule Sleep into headlines. The work I love most, though, happens before any marketing campaign or pitch goes out: sitting with a founder and figuring out what they actually stand for. I know how reputations get built.

Almost all of my business has always come from referrals. In 2020, I started treating myself more like a client and following the advice I always give: build relationships before you need them, with people who’ll gladly vouch for you. I gave more talks, presented on webinars, spoke on conference panels and launched my newsletter. My favorite was a webinar I gave for MBA and EMBA students through BlueSteps called “LinkedIn Tips for Personal Branding.”

It’s paid off, and it started with being more selective and intentional.

#5250. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

Learn more about the technology making it all work.
