#5249. There are now more centimillionaires at Anthropic than in all of L.A. thanks to its IPO—staff gained a total of $430 billion overnight

Anthropic’s 5,300 employees are starting a new week with more money than they could fathom just days ago.

The company’s IPO sent its collective employee wealth soaring, putting the average non-founder staff’s estimated fortune at more than $44 million. But for 598 non-founder employees, they now have at least $100 million to their name, according to a report by private-markets investing firm Hill, cited by Reuters.

That means Anthropic has more centimillionaires among its ranks than there are living in the entirety of London, Paris, or Los Angeles. The only cities with more are San Francisco and New York City, according to wealth migration firm Henley & Partners.

Those estimates are based on Anthropic’s $83-per-share IPO price, a level the stock has yet to fall below. By Thursday’s close, shares had climbed to $97.17, putting the collective estimated wealth of Anthropic’s employees and seven cofounders at roughly $433 billion—more wealth than the entire bottom one-third of Americans, according to a viral analysis by Steve Rattner.

While Anthropic shares have since pulled back to around $88—making the total Anthropic staff equity closer to $350 billion—the wealth gains remain substantial.

Anthropic’s rise after being founded in 2021 has been meteoric. But critics have warned that the wealth generated by its rapid growth is also raising questions about who stands to benefit from the AI boom—and who could be left behind.

Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who appeared at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum earlier this month, said changes need to be made to the tax code so that so much wealth cannot be preserved among a few people.

“AI has the potential to create enormous prosperity. But if all that wealth flows to a handful of people at the top while working families struggle to get ahead, we’re not building an economy of the future,” he posted on X. “We’re repeating the mistakes of the past.”

Hana Ivanhoe, senior manager of private sector campaigns and advocacy at anti-poverty nonprofit Oxfam America, echoed to Fortune that Anthropic’s IPO offers a striking example of how the AI boom could deepen existing economic divides.

“The level of wealth concentration that Anthropic’s IPO has precipitated is obviously jarring, and it’s emblematic of the extreme inequality that already characterizes our economy and is sure to be exacerbated by future IPOs like this one,” she said.

That wealth is being generated amid growing questions about AI’s breakneck pace of development and its potential consequences for the job market—and even humanity itself.

“It’s not only a problem that these IPOs are making a rich few even richer, it’s that they are getting richer at the expense of everyone else,” Ivanhoe added. “There’s both wealth inequality and inequality of impact at play here.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s net worth skyrocketed to some $21 billion with the IPO, but he has also voiced concerns about the consequences of AI driving that wealth.

“The thing to worry about is a level of wealth concentration that will break society,” he wrote in a letter released in January.

In response, Amodei, alongside his fellow six founders, committed to donate 80% of their Anthropic equity to philanthropy—and urged others to be more generous with their giving.

And while Amodei has also called for the AI industry to slow down development amid his own concerns about AI systems going rogue, being used in cyberattacks and bioterrorism, or causing serious economic disruption, Anthropic went through with its IPO, in part, because of a need for more financing to develop AI safely. Competitor OpenAI delayed its IPO until 2027.

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5248. CZ Sounds Alarm as Japan Orders Crackdown on ID Data Storage

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, has expressed his concerns about the storage of sensitive personal data after Japanese authorities called on rental car services to delete customers' identity documents following a massive data breach.

In his latest X post, CZ pointed to a Nov. 18 notice issued by Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). The notice urges rental car services to be cautious about unnecessarily storing images of driver’s licenses and other government-issued identification documents.

The recent call by Japanese authorities comes after a massive cybersecurity attack on a popular Japanese car-sharing service called Times Car, operated by Park24 Group.

The incident began when the company noticed suspicious activity on its system on Sept. 25. As a result, it launched an investigation into whether someone had accessed its systems without permission, potentially exposing customer data.

As per the disclosure by Park24 on Oct. 23, about 6.63 million customer accounts were impacted by the breach.

Worse, the investigation uncovered evidence that hackers had transmitted 1,464,800 encrypted images of identification documents, including driver’s licenses, to external locations.

Besides that, another 891,602 encrypted images of identification documents were accessed suspiciously. However, investigators found no evidence that these additional ID images had been transmitted outside the company’s systems.

Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission issued its notice on Nov. 18, focusing on the risks of retaining sensitive personal data even after its original purpose has been fulfilled.

The regulatory body stressed that storing unnecessary identification images could significantly worsen the consequences of cyberattacks.

Although Japan’s latest warning specifically targets the rental car industry, CZ’s decision to share his concerns about this issue also raises questions about personal data protection in the crypto industry.

Generally, centralized crypto exchanges require users to go through a Know Your Customer (KYC) process to access their trading platforms.

Depending on the platform and jurisdiction, these processes may require users to provide photos of their passports, driver’s licenses, national ID cards, and other sensitive information.

This kind of sensitive data can be a goldmine for cybercriminals, who can exploit stolen personal information for various activities such as identity theft, phishing attacks, fraudulent registrations, and more

#5247. Your Customers Just Got an AI Agent. Is Your Business Ready to Talk to Them?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Personal AI agents are now customers. Here’s how businesses can prepare.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

There’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very important questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

From the consumer’s perspective, a personal agent fights the battles they don’t want to, and does so more rigorously than they ever could.

Someone’s flight gets cancelled, and their personal agent can argue with the airline until it gets a credit. Someone points it at subscription services and gets every one to offer a discounted rate. I’ve seen dozens of these examples pile up on social media over the past few weeks, and the pattern is always the same. A task a person would normally decide was not worth the trouble is now getting done anyway, because an agent has no concept of trouble.

We used to think about bots talking to bots like something that will happen “someday.” It’s happening now. For consumers who don’t want to solve problems through sheer persistence and patience, this is an exciting development. For businesses that have built their customer service programs around interacting with humans, this is a challenge to solve, fast.

The simple response to this innovation sounds like: “We need our policies to be accurate, because AI will be better at calling us out on them than a human customer.” It goes deeper than that. Every refund policy and guarantee clause has fine print and phrases that are ever so slightly open to interpretation. Personal AI agents can read these policies and find where they bend in ways a human never could.

And they’ll do this at scale. One customer raising a question and finding a loophole is a cost of doing business. Thousands of agents doing the same thing can overwhelm a business, both financially and operationally.

That kind of volume does not behave like a normal surge in customer support demand. It behaves more like a denial-of-service attack. Nobody debates whether each individual request is legitimate; the volume itself is the problem. The response has to be infrastructural: detecting, filtering, a real system for deciding what gets through. “We will deal with it when it happens” is not a strategy at this scale.

Retail and travel may seem like the industries most vulnerable to risk, but any business with documented policies faces the same exposure. Insurance, financial services, healthcare — wherever a company has put a promise or statement of intent in writing, an agent can find it and act on it.

AI has already carved out a massive role in how businesses interact with customers. Now it’s showing up on the other side of the conversation. Nobody has every single answer for how to prepare for this new reality, us included. But there are foundational moves worth making now, rather than waiting for the rest of the industry to decide what to do.

First, there’s the question of identity. Most businesses have no reliable way to know whether they are talking to a customer, a customer’s authorized agent or something pretending to be one. That infrastructure needs to be in place before anything else matters.

Second, you need visibility into what is already happening. You need to be able to see how often an agent is showing up in a support queue, what it’s asking for and how often it’s succeeding.

Then there’s the issue of the policies themselves. A traditional review to ensure accuracy is no longer sufficient. Businesses need to audit their policies, line by line, and stress-test every potential ambiguity that could turn into a vulnerability. Find the gaps before an agent does.

Resist the instinct to default to blocking. Throughout history, we’ve seen what happens to companies that try to close a door that’s going to be kicked down regardless. Search engines that tried to wall off the open web lost to the ones that stayed open, and the same pattern is likely to repeat here. Open does not mean undefended. It means building real verification and governance instead of a blanket “no,” even while the rest of the playbook is still being written.

Big players are picking sides right now, with Amazon blocking personal agents and Shopify building a lane. It’s tempting to treat their moves as a test case, something to monitor from the sidelines until the winds blow in one definitive direction.

That would be a mistake. Sure, the headlines may change in a week; in the case of these specific AI agents and the companies that created them, there may be developments that complicate their rapid surge in the short term. But the shift is happening, and CX organizations can’t be lulled into a reactive posture.

Nobody has built the perfect system for this yet. But the companies spending this period of uncertainty getting their infrastructure ready will be the ones with real footing when the dust settles. Everyone else will still be reading the news, wondering what to do next.

Right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

There’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very important questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

#5246. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5245. Can AI Hack Smart Contracts? How AI Agents Are Changing Blockchain Security

Smart contract vulnerability scanners typically work by looking for certain patterns. However, because an AI agent can iterate and make use of dependencies, local blockchain forks, and decompilation, it weakens the protection gained by keeping source code secret, and can attempt attacks against complex vulnerabilities such as access control bugs, accounting errors, oracle-related bugs and unexpected contract interactions.

For example, in December 2025, Anthropic released results from SCONE-bench, a smart contract benchmark of 405 contracts that were exploited in the 2020 - 2025 period. They were able to reproduce exploits for 207 contracts, totalling $550.1 million (simulated stolen funds).

To make sure the agent was not simply memorising exploits that were already published, newer vulnerabilities that had been published after their training cutoff were tested on Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5, which were able to generate $4.6 million (simulated stolen funds).

Finally, they analysed 2,849 recent smart contracts with no known issues, discovering two previously unknown vulnerabilities that could have resulted in $3,694 (simulated stolen funds), emphasising the ability of AI agents to discover new vulnerabilities rather than simply exploiting known ones.

Anthropic emphasised that no actual funds were lost during these experiments. It should also be noted that in one of their experiments using GPT-5, it cost $3,476 for API usage, which leaves a slim (simulated) profit.

With automated hacking becoming more effective, how can we be sure that DeFi will be able to stay ahead of these AI agents? Hacken, a blockchain security firm, reported that $1.18 billion was lost in 107 crypto hacks during the third quarter of 2026. 48% of this was from exploiting smart contracts.

Of course, this doesn’t specify the cause of these hacks. Regardless, it emphasises the importance of being able to stay ahead of AIs which could be used for exploitation.

Chainalysis estimates that approximately $36.7 million was stolen in 2026 from DeFi protocols that had not undergone smart contract verification. It also notes AI-assisted reverse engineering as an emerging risk without attributing any particular thefts to AI.

In an experiment by a16z on 20 past DeFi price manipulation exploits, apparent success rates of 50% were reduced to 10% when the researchers restricted access to transactional data that revealed the original exploit. When the researchers gave the AI some high-level information about the DeFi domain, success rates jumped to 70%.

In February 2026, OpenAI and Paradigm released a benchmark for evaluating agents’ abilities in the domains of vulnerability detection, patching, and exploitation using an EVM environment (EVMbench). Results showed that GPT-5.3-Codex achieved a 71% success rate in exploitation (limited to a sandboxed environment) and 33.3% for GPT-5.

In October 2026, CyberChainBench was released, analyzing 541 exploit events across 9 Ethereum-compatible blockchains. The best-performing configuration achieved 37.5%, 43.7%, and 23.4% success rates for detection, exploitation, and patching respectively.

In a simulation, the best-performing agent profited $57.4 million from exploits on 200 exploit events that occurred after the cutoff. Some of the reported high-severity issues were evaluated and determined to not be exploitable by OpenZeppelin. Since much of the data is trained on in the public, results may be exaggerated.

Agents will continue to improve, and while current results are not an indication that AI-driven agents are responsible for large scale on-chain thefts, it is an indication that AI can find and exploit weaknesses in smart contracts given a certain environment. Given the ease with which agents can try attacking many different protocols, smaller protocols may see an uptick in exploit attempts.

Teams that implement rigorous testing and monitoring could have an edge over other teams. For example, AI could be used to test a contract prior to deployment, generate regression tests, and identify weird behavior on-chain. A human would still need to verify any potential issues and sign off on changes.

Teams should continue to perform third-party audits and implement other security best practices such as limiting access to sensitive information, setting up alerts and response plans, restricting the amount of money in a wallet, making sure AI systems do not have permissions to transact without human oversight where necessary, and so on.

#5244. He Retired at 50. At 70, He’s Working 7 Days a Week on His Biggest Idea Yet.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Peter Castleman could have spent retirement playing golf — instead, he built WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform.

If you’re like me, your approach to nutrition mostly involves squinting at a label, not recognizing any of the ingredients, and eating the thing anyway. Peter Castleman decided that wasn’t good enough. After four decades as an investor, including as Chairman and Managing Partner of J.H. Whitney & Co., where he played a role in investments tied to The North Face, Igloo and Herbalife, Peter came out of retirement to become the founder and CEO of WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform that has mapped more than 840,000 products. He’s 70 years old and says he’s never felt more excited about an idea, proving it’s never too late to chase a big idea.

Give us the elevator pitch. What is WISEcode?Basically, we’re trying to solve what I call the food information crisis. We literally don’t know two things: what’s in our food and what it does to us. At WISEcode, we’ve been spending a dozen years or so solving that. We’ve created what we call the Food Genome Project, which is really mapping the entire food system. So we now know exactly what’s in our foods, and we can tell you what it does for you. And that applies to consumers, policymakers, government people, industries, retailers, scientists, everyone. That information didn’t exist, and now it does.

This isn’t the first company you’ve started or been a big part of. Why did you want to become a founder again?Well, I’m 70, okay? When I turned 50, I retired from my firm. I’m healthy. I eat generally well. But when you turn 50, you enter the kill zone for chronic disease, and chronic disease is 90% of our health issues, and 80% of chronic disease is driven by what we choose to do. We actually control most of our health outcomes. So I basically wanted to simply hack what I’m going to eat. I didn’t want to get cognitive issues. I didn’t want to get any late-onset chronic disease. But that hack doesn’t exist. It shocked me. It just doesn’t exist. So this passion became the business purpose of WISEcode, and I said, “Okay, I’m gonna get this information. I’m going to do for me, I’m going to do for every single individual. I’m going to give them Food Truth.” Formally, I’ve probably been doing this for about 12, 13 years. Informally, I’ve been thinking about it for 20 years.

When a business is a personal passion, do you have a process for figuring out whether it will be a passion for other people, too? Or do you just follow your heart?Like many people, I suffer from that latter part, which is letting your emotions get too far into stuff. I’ve always said, “Fall in love with your family and your friends, not your businesses.” It’s hard to do, because you develop passions. I have three tests I generally apply to any kind of activity. The first I call the North Star test: is it very clear that what you’re trying to do resonates with others? Is it going to be an aha moment or a so-what moment to the world? Number two, I call the sandbox test. How big is your sandbox? How big is your addressable market? And how crowded is your sandbox? And then the third one I call the moat test, which is: can you build defensible business assets that prevent people from copying what you do? People will copy you in a second if you’re successful. If I’m not slam-dunk strong on all three tests, I try to stay away. I apply that to WISEcode. I apply it to everything I do. I’m better at it now than I was at 25.

How do you figure out if other people are interested in your idea when you don’t have a big budget?Social media and everything we have today are double-edged swords. But I use SurveyMonkey all the time. You can ask a question and, for not very much money, you can get 500, 1,000 really clear answers that help you evolve. You can do the same thing on social media tools. The tools out there today are so great. It used to be you’d have to hire McKinsey or Bain for a gazillion dollars, and they’d do a six-month study. Now, in a day, you can get better information than they ever gave you.

What do you say to someone in their 50s who thinks, “I always wanted to do my own thing, but it’s too late”?First and foremost, I think you gotta be honest with yourself. Who are you? What do you love doing, and are you good at this? Late in your career, any time, if you don’t have the energy, the drive and the staying power, don’t do it. Because building companies is hard. You’re going to get knocked on your fanny a ton of times. You gotta get back up. You gotta inspire others around you. You gotta keep going when everyone says, “Don’t do it.” You’re gonna run out of money. You’re gonna have your spouse saying, “What the hell are you doing?” But if it’s in your DNA, it’s the greatest thing in the world. Most of my contemporaries are reducing their handicap on the golf course, and I’m spending 10 hours a day, seven days a week on WISEcode, and I love it. I wouldn’t change it for the world, but that’s me. The greatest joy I get, besides my love of my friends and family, is building businesses that actually make a difference, and if that’s in your DNA, do it. I think the only failure in life is not trying.

#5243. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

#5241. XRP Flashes Biggest Volatility Warning Among Major Cryptocurrencies

XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data. The options market indicates that traders are now preparing for price swings that could be nearly double XRP's historical seven-day price move.

XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median. This figure far exceeds similar metrics for major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL).

XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility. Solana shows the lowest premium among these four cryptocurrencies, Coinbase remarked.

As the chart below indicates, the options-implied seven-day price move for XRP is around 9.6%, according to Glassnode and Coinbase data as of Nov. 17. This compares to its historical median absolute price move of about 4.9%.

Basically, this means that the options market is signaling a price swing nearly twice as large as XRP's typical seven-day price movement.

Interestingly, Solana's implied price move is also close to 9.5%, almost the same as XRP's. Yet its historical median weekly price move is much higher at about 6.5%.

The key here is that although both cryptocurrencies exhibit similarly large potential price moves, the magnitude of the expected volatility surprise is significantly greater for XRP relative to its usual trading range.

For comparison, Bitcoin shows an options-implied seven-day move of about 6%, versus its historical median of about 3.5%. For Ethereum, these numbers are about 8% and 5.1%, respectively.

Obviously, this latest figure doesn't necessarily imply that XRP is going to crash. It's a sign that options traders expect a big price move regardless of its direction.

Implied volatility is a forward-looking measure. It's based on options prices. The higher the implied volatility, the more traders pay for exposure to potential price movements or protection against them.

The chart from Coinbase is based on a one-standard-deviation estimate. It's derived by converting annualized at-the-money implied volatility into a seven-day timeframe.

For XRP, the roughly 9.6% implied move represents a statistical range. It's not a guaranteed price target. A one-standard-deviation range suggests about a 68% chance of the price staying within this range under typical modeling assumptions.

Thus, the latest figure of 1.94x implies that XRP's volatility premium remains high despite a slight decrease from the previous reading.

From XRP traders' perspective, this can be a very challenging market environment. For traders using leverage, there could be a high risk of liquidation due to potentially sharp price moves.

Orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

#5238. StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

StepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

StepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company says it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

#5237. Bitcoin (BTC) Demand Hits 2026 Low as Price Retests $62,000

Bitcoin is facing increased fear and panic among traders as its price volatility continues to intensify, causing both retail and institutional investors to move with caution.

While Bitcoin is still struggling to regain momentum amid the persistent market downturn, the latest on-chain data from CryptoQuant shows that Bitcoin's demand has dropped to its weakest level in 2026.

The data shows that Bitcoin's apparent demand is rapidly showing signs of weakness, with the metric dropping below -290,000 BTC before seeing a brief recovery to about -255,000 BTC as of November 18.

However, this does not provide any relief, as Bitcoin’s apparent demand remains substantially below its monthly average of around -172,000 BTC.

As such, it appears that investors’ interest in accumulating Bitcoin remains significantly subdued by the fear of potential losses. Hence, investors are growing increasingly cautious about entering the market amid the rising selling pressure.

The data shows that investors are growing increasingly wary of their Bitcoin positions amid growing uncertainty about its potential price movements, as Bitcoin’s price downturn has only intensified over the past few days.

While the asset’s price has dipped further, Bitcoin has suddenly retested $62,000 as of November 18, a price level last seen during the severe price crash in July.

Nonetheless, further data shows that it has briefly recovered to $63,817.43 as of the time of writing, showing a decline of about 1.12% over the past 24 hours.

Despite Bitcoin’s extremely negative demand and weak price movements, market analysts are still positive about a potential reversal, describing the moment as an opportunity to buy at a lower price.

It has been previously observed that while many investors are becoming increasingly bearish, periods of widespread fear can sometimes flush out weaker hands, thereby triggering a change in market direction.

#5236. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.)

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on a deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and others aren’t built to process.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

Angela Gunn is a GRC consultant and vCISO with Ericius Security. She has worked in infosec and incident response roles for companies including Microsoft, HP and BAE Systems Applied Intelligence. Prior to working in the tech sector, she covered it as a journalist for publications including USA Today, PC Magazine, Computerworld, Yahoo! Internet Life and Seattle Weekly.

#5235. I Stayed On a Private Island in Fiji. It Pulls Off a Top Travel Trend With a Luxury Twist—Here’s What Any Hospitality Business Can Learn.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Kokomo Private Island offers a bespoke experience guests will dream about long after they return home.

When Lang Walker, the late Australian billionaire property developer and philanthropist, and his wife, Sue Walker, first saw Yaukuve Levu Island, Kadavu, Fiji, surrounded by the Great Astrolabe Reef, the land was largely overgrown, with the remains of a development that had never been completed.

“We anchored the boat out the front, looked at it and thought what a wonderful place this could be,” Sue Walker recalls. “It took eight years and an enormous amount of hard work to bring that vision to life.”

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

Today, the property features 21 beachfront villas and five hilltop residences, each with a private pool; three principal dining venues, with more than 80% of herbs and greens sourced from the island’s 5.5-acre organic farm; the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with its dedicated fitness center; and no shortage of adventure and cultural activities available to its guests.

My husband and I had a chance to experience the tropical island paradise for ourselves in September. Throughout our stay, we were struck by Kokomo’s sheer natural beauty and how much the luxury hospitality experience was rooted in a genuine sense of place.

Increasingly, hotels and resorts highlighting local character rise to the top of travelers’ wishlists. Nearly three-quarters of luxury travelers won’t pay for accommodations that feel generic, per a report from Preferred Hotels & Resorts, and 77% of travelers prioritize authentic experiences representative of local culture, according to research from Booking.com.

Kokomo serves as a lesson in hospitality excellence — what it takes to succeed in a travel landscape increasingly defined by a desire for authenticity and local character. Here’s how every business can do the same.

After a long day (or more) of travel, first impressions are key. Guests want to feel at ease and an immediate sense of place. But, sometimes, that’s the straightforward part. Sustaining that genuine warm welcome throughout the stay also matters.

Staff members at Kokomo give it its personality and make guests feel at home, often forming relationships that bring people back year after year, Walker says.

Additionally, Kokomo has developed a close relationship with the local community, where some staff members are from: supporting local employment, working with neighboring villages, and contributing to education, healthcare and community initiatives.

“Authenticity comes from allowing those relationships and traditions to exist naturally, rather than trying to manufacture an experience for guests,” Walker says. “When someone shares a story about their village, introduces a guest to a local custom or folklore or even simply welcomes them with genuine Fijian hospitality, that’s what stays with people.”

Our arrival and journey to Kokomo was seamless from the first “bula” (Fijian for “hello” and a wish for life and good health). After a 45-minute seaplane ride, we touched down on the crystalline blue waters in front of Kokomo. We were given a salusalu, a traditional garland worn around the neck, and coconut water, and listened to a group of staff members sing traditional Fijian welcome songs.

That warmth and hospitality extended throughout our time at Kokomo, across the interactions we had with staff and when we visited the nearby Dravuni Village, which is home to a small indigenous Fijian community. We heard traditional songs, learned about their hand-woven crafts, participated in a kava ceremony and toured the village with a staff member who’d grown up there.

The business lesson is this: Lean into what makes a destination special, and the cultural touchstones that define it, for an authentic welcome that extends from the first moment to the last.

Of course, as much as people want to soak up all a destination has to offer, they’ll spend a good portion of their vacation in their accommodations. Ideally, those accommodations capture the destination’s unique characteristics while prioritizing comfort.

“For me, true luxury isn’t about formality,” Walker says. “It’s about comfort, freedom, being able to enjoy yourself without feeling constrained by the usual expectations of a hotel. Children should be able to run around, explore and have adventures, while their parents and grandparents can relax and enjoy the island in their own way.”

Our one-bedroom beachfront villa, just steps from the ocean, felt sprung from the tropical landscape itself. The high ceilings, neutral stone and wood, and ample windows, the better to display the expansive patio with its private pool and the dazzling ocean view, created an indoor-outdoor flow with understated natural elegance.

When it comes to architecture, interior design, or landscape, embracing what sets the place surrounding it apart from any other, rather than competing with it, helps establish that seamless, one-of-kind experience guests won’t forget.

Whether a guest is a serious gourmet or not, meals will stand out as part of the experience (a three-times-a-day touchpoint). For remote resorts where guests rely solely on the dining on-site, it’s even more critical to deliver elevated, locally-defined experiences.

Early on, the Walkers realized they had access to the best ingredients on their doorstep — fresh seafood and the climate and space to grow much of the island’s own produce — and built their culinary philosophy around that, Walker says.

“A fish caught locally that morning, vegetables picked from the garden, herbs cut just before they’re used,” she explains. “You can’t get much fresher than that. Building and operating a resort in such a remote location comes with enormous logistical challenges, so growing more of our own food and reducing our reliance on imported produce makes sense on many levels.”

We had a chance to go on a tour with Kokomo’s executive chef Marty Kindleysides. He gave us an inside look at the island’s farm and hydroponic gardens, which help shape the menus across its restaurants: the Beach Shack on Kokomo’s western beach; Walker D’Plank, featuring Asian-influenced cuisine, near the arrival jetty; and the poolside Kokocabana, highlighting Italian-inspired dishes.

From the beautiful lunch Kindleysides prepared for us with farm-fresh ingredients like squash and kale, to all of the meals we enjoyed at the other dining venues, including a showstopping dinner by Chef Caroline during a curry-themed night at Walker D’Plank, the food was flavorful, intentional and reinforced a singular dining experience.

Guests should never feel like the food where they’re staying is an afterthought; it’s another opportunity — and a very memorable one — to showcase innovation and what makes a setting unique.

At a remote tropical resort like Kokomo, guests have the luxury of a picture-perfect natural setting offering once-in-a-lifetime activities. But striking the balance between making the most of the environment and protecting it is also critical.

Lang was an avid diver for most of his life and immediately recognized the wonder of the Great Astrolabe Reef. The Walkers saw it as their responsibility to look after it, so they set out to help guests experience and understand it.

“There’s something quite powerful about a child helping to plant coral, or a family learning about the individual manta rays that return to our waterways each season,” Walker says. “Suddenly conservation becomes personal. You’re no longer looking at a beautiful reef, rather, you’re beginning to understand how it works and why protecting it matters.”

We had the opportunity to meet with a marine biologist to learn about the manta rays and conservation efforts. Kokomo has partnered with Manta Project Fiji to research and protect Fiji’s reef manta rays since 2017. More than 500 manta ray sightings were recorded during the most recent monitoring period. We even went to look for them by boat, but unfortunately with it being the tail end of the season, didn’t spot any.

Additionally, the marine biologist led us on a guided coral restoration tour, where we snorkeled over some of the current projects underway. More than 2,000 corals have been transplanted as part of Kokomo’s coral restoration. The island also has six active coral nurseries, which can support more than 10,000 corals per season.

Bringing guests into the very projects that protect the place they’re staying gives them destination-driven, extraordinary experiences while safeguarding them for future generations.

Relaxation means different things to different people, but centralizing spa and wellness options in one place, and melding personalized comfort with distinct ambiance, gives everyone the option to design an ideal routine to reset.

The Walkers wanted to build on the feeling guests have upon arrival — everyday life demands removed by the grandeur of nature — and developed the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with that in mind.

We enjoyed Kokomo’s signature “Pacific Mastery Massage,” which incorporates centuries-old methods from traditional Fijian Bobo, combining variable pressure and rhythmic movement with the preferred oil blend. Before and after the service, we sipped iced hibiscus tea (the flower is often seen in Fijian landscaping) in the garden setting.

Guests will remember how a vacation makes them feel, so making sure they have the option to truly unwind, whatever that looks like for them, is key. Infusing it with a local twist means they won’t forget exactly where they experienced it.

At the end of the stay, as we departed on the one-hour helicopter ride back to the hangar, spotting our villa on the lush island encircled by a shock of turquoise, we came away already nostalgic for the trip, and with a deeper appreciation for Fiji’s natural beauty and vibrant culture.

We would love to return some day (maybe to snorkel with the mantas) — and that’s exactly what the Walkers intended.

“More than anything, I hope guests leave Kokomo feeling they’ve been part of something special,” Walker says. “That they’ve spent quality time with the people they love, experienced the generosity of our Fijian team and discovered a part of the world they’ll always remember. If they leave feeling as though Kokomo is their island home, then we’ve achieved what we set out to do.”

When Lang Walker, the late Australian billionaire property developer and philanthropist, and his wife, Sue Walker, first saw Yaukuve Levu Island, Kadavu, Fiji, surrounded by the Great Astrolabe Reef, the land was largely overgrown, with the remains of a development that had never been completed.

“We anchored the boat out the front, looked at it and thought what a wonderful place this could be,” Sue Walker recalls. “It took eight years and an enormous amount of hard work to bring that vision to life.”

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

#5234. 17 Years Ago, Satoshi Nakamoto Opens His BitcoinTalk Account: What Happened Next

On this day, 17 years ago, Satoshi Nakamoto opened an account on BitcoinTalk, the place that would become the home of early Bitcoin enthusiasts and then turn into a public forum for crypto in general, until social media platforms took over the internet.

The network itself was barely 1 year old, and its future raised more questions than answers. Satoshi Nakamoto welcomed users on the forum and invited any questions people had regarding the cryptocurrency.

In 2010, the revolution began: 10,000 BTC was used to buy two pizzas, one of the first uses of the digital asset in exchange for a commodity. In May, Laszlo Hanyecz probably had the most expensive pizza dinner in history, considering how much BTC rallied after that. By December, Satoshi made their final BitcoinTalk post and announced their farewell.

The 2011-2014 period turned out to be the foundation for the network as a whole. Bitcoin became an open-source project maintained by others. The first halving happened in November 2012 and reduced the block issuance from 50 to 25 BTC per block.

The first-ever exchange implosion, Mt.Gox in 2014, raised serious questions about the security and stability of centralized exchanges, an issue we haven't solved 17 years later.

2017-2021 were the years when the industry truly blossomed. We had our first bull run on Bitcoin, which pushed the price above expected levels, to almost $20,000 in December 2017, along with the first altcoin bull run and the birth of new technologies like smart contracts, NFTs and many more. The next cycle took Bitcoin to around $69,000 in November 2021.

However, with the growth of the industry, multiple conflicts arose around safety, integrity and usage. The first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin was El Salvador, which implemented the digital currency as a true means of payment, in addition to accumulating it in its treasury.

2022 was the pivotal year, marked by the FTX and Terra crashes that changed how investors treat markets in general. FTX wasn't just an exchange: it was the backbone of the cryptocurrency market in those years. It aimed to rival Binance and become the bridge between institutional investors and crypto.

However, poor risk management, issues with fund allocation and many other factors caused an implosion that ended the bull run.

In 2024, Wall Street arrived in crypto with ETFs, ETPs, perpetual futures and a regulatory framework. The digital assets industry became a part of a larger market. Whether that is good or bad is a question to consider, but one thing is clear: Bitcoin has come a very long way since 2010 and is evolving to this day.

The next step is the arrival of AI and rising cybersecurity risks, which go toe-to-toe with the quantum danger. How the first cryptocurrency handles them is a question that directly affects its future.

#5233. Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am

A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.
