#5231. AI Is Accelerating Software Development — But Businesses Need a Better Way to Measure the Quality of What They Ship

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI-assisted development has quietly made the metrics boards rely on unreliable.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

By 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

Two major datasets show how far the dashboard has drifted from reality:

On a typical board dashboard, the throughput gains appear as headline numbers while the instability sits in a footnote. A director reading deployment frequency would see an organization getting faster, with no view of the review process thinning out underneath it.

DORA has acknowledged the gap. Its researchers introduced deployment rework rate, the proportion of deployments that are unplanned fixes, as a fifth measure in 2024. DORA’s Nathen Harvey said on DX’s Engineering Enablement podcast that the four keys aren’t sufficient on their own for understanding AI’s impact.

Rework rate is worth tracking, but it records the fix only after a customer has already hit the bug. It can’t warn you before a release.

Code coverage reports how much of a codebase some test executed. It says nothing about whether that test checked an outcome a customer cares about, and AI-generated test suites can push coverage up without improving that second question.

A suite can touch every branch of a checkout service and still never confirm that a customer paying in a second currency gets charged the right amount.

You build verification coverage from the customer side. Product, engineering and finance agree on the journeys that make or lose money: signup, checkout, the core action the product exists for and the permission flows enterprise buyers probe during procurement.

Each journey gets an expected outcome written in business terms, such as an order confirmed at the correct price or an invited user landing with the right role. For each release, the team records how many of those journeys it ran end to end on the release candidate, in real browsers and devices, and how many produced that outcome.

A CFO can read the result without a glossary: something like “47 of 52 revenue-critical journeys verified before release.” Because your team measures it before anything ships, it should move ahead of rework rate and change failure rate, which register problems only after customers find them.

Part of the pressure comes from outside engineering. Cyber underwriters have started asking CFOs how they are managing AI risk.

Directors who signed off on AI tooling budgets will also start asking what the spend bought besides volume. A rising deployment count tells them the team ships more often. Verification coverage tells them whether the product customers pay for still works.

Most teams can produce a first figure within a quarter by following four steps:

Agentic test automation platforms such as KaneAI now let teams run these journeys against the rendered product on every release candidate.

DORA metrics still belong on the dashboard, because they tell you how fast and how steadily your organization delivers. Add verification coverage beside them in your next monthly report, and protect it from the pressure every board metric attracts.

A team under pressure can raise its score by shortening the journey list. Require product and finance sign-off before anyone changes it, and show the list size next to the ratio.

Include the failure cases customers hit, such as a declined card or an expired session, because a journey verified only on its happy path tells the board less than the number suggests.

Expect the score to sit below 100%, and tell directors which journeys failed and why. When they ask what AI has changed, you can show them how much of what shipped was verified to work.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

By 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

Major crypto exchange Coinbase shared the options-implied seven-day ratios for major cryptocurrencies, highlighting that options traders might be preparing for an unusually large price move for XRP.

In an X post, Coinbase Markets shared the outcome of dividing the options-implied 7-day move by the median 7-day move for XRP, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana.

Options-implied 7d move, divided by each asset's own median 7d move: $XRP 1.94× $BTC 1.69× $ETH 1.56× $SOL 1.46× $XRP is priced furthest above its own history, $SOL the least. Which one is asking for more than its own history delivered? https://t.co/WgWbqjcgwI

This suggests how much movement options markets are pricing in relative to each asset's own historical behavior. However, it does not compare their expected dollar or percentage moves directly.

According to the figures shared by Coinbase, XRP's options-implied seven-day move stands at 1.94 times its own historical median seven-day move. Bitcoin follows at 1.69 times, while Ethereum records 1.56 times and Solana comes in at 1.46 times.

XRP, therefore has the highest relative reading among the four assets, suggesting options traders are pricing in a more pronounced move than the token has typically delivered over a comparable period.

At the time of writing, XRP was down 1.93% in the last 24 hours to $0.98 amid the continued profit-taking in the market. XRP briefly reached $1 on November 18, 2026, but fell afterwards as traders took profits. XRP is down 21.57% so far in November, but its history says more than its current price action does.

XRP’s average November gain is skewed upward by massive outlier rallies—specifically +550% in 2013 and +282% in 2024. Its median November return is about -10%, meaning it has closed lower in most cycles in history. XRP dropped roughly 23.42% in November 2019 and lost 12.18% in November 2025 (opening at around $2.51 and closing at around $2.20).

A weak November doesn’t always mean a weak December: for instance, after falling 9.1% in November 2015, XRP jumped 46.8% in December 2015.

In the near term, XRP’s price recovery will target $1 before moving to the $1.24–$1.26 range. Alternatively, if the price falls further, it is likely to find support at $0.89.

#5229. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

#5228. 5 Powerful Lessons Leaders Can Learn From People Who Pay It Forward

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Five leadership lessons on measuring the long-term value of investing in people.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

I founded the William S.D. Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind. Over the next three decades, I watched scholars build careers, support families and, in many cases, create opportunities for others. This year, the Foundation sought to understand those outcomes more systematically. It surveyed and interviewed former scholars, publishing its findings in a white paper, Opening Doors Through Education. The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

The findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. Former scholars described how their education helped them build careers, improve their families’ circumstances and contribute to their communities. Many have also gone on to support others through mentoring, volunteering and philanthropy, extending the benefits of their education to people they may never have reached otherwise.

While the research is exploratory and cannot establish cause and effect, it raises questions that extend well beyond philanthropy. Every organization invests in people, yet few measure what those investments make possible over a lifetime. Here are five lessons I believe leaders can take from our experience.

The paper introduces a measure called the William Louey Effect: the difference between the path a scholar actually followed and the one that might reasonably have been expected given their starting circumstances. The name matters less than the question behind it: compared with what?

Businesses regularly celebrate employees who complete leadership programs and subsequently earn promotions. But would those employees have succeeded without the training? A talented person who was already destined to thrive tells us relatively little about the program. Someone whose trajectory genuinely changed tells us considerably more.

Leaders should examine starting circumstances, not simply final achievements. Otherwise, they risk rewarding programs for identifying talent rather than developing it.

One of our paper’s most striking findings is also among its most uncertain. It estimates that parental income is approximately 46% less predictive of our scholars’ adult earnings than it is nationally in China, comparing coefficients of 0.27 and 0.50. But that estimate draws on income ranges reported by roughly 10 people, all originally selected for academic promise. Some of the difference might have existed without our support.

The same problem affects corporate high-potential programs. When participants outperform their peers, how much credit belongs to the program, and how much to the selection process? Good measurement requires intellectual humility. Leaders should distinguish between outcomes they observe and impact they can reasonably attribute to their intervention. Acknowledging uncertainty does not weaken a success story. It makes the conclusions more credible.

From the beginning, I encouraged scholars to pay their opportunities forward when they felt ready, whether through money, knowledge or time. I never wanted that expectation to become a condition of receiving support. The paper calls this voluntary reciprocity: giving that emerges from gratitude and personal conviction rather than contractual obligation.

Organizations often seek loyalty through retention bonuses, repayment clauses and restrictive agreements. Such mechanisms can serve legitimate purposes, but they cannot manufacture genuine commitment. Some of our earliest scholars independently established and funded a scholarship for Chinese students at Oxford. We did not require them to do so, because when people feel trusted rather than indebted, they have the freedom to turn an opportunity they received into something of their own.

Generosity becomes more powerful when people can see what it looks like. Several scholars who established the Oxford scholarship also mentor its recipients, offering guidance similar to the support they once received. They are passing forward not only financial resources, but a way of treating people.

The leadership lesson is practical. If you want employees to mentor colleagues, share knowledge and create opportunities, make those expectations visible through your own behavior. Take time to advise younger employees, introduce promising people to contacts who can help them, and continue supporting colleagues even when there is no immediate benefit to you. Then give others the freedom to contribute in their own ways.

A culture of generosity cannot be built through instructions alone. It grows when people repeatedly experience the behavior their leaders advocate.

We have never asked a scholar to repay their scholarship. Instead, many have supported relatives, mentored students or helped others pursue opportunities. One former scholar described the experience as bringing philanthropy forward by a generation. For business leaders, this suggests a broader definition of return on investment.

Consider an employee who leaves your company and becomes an exceptional manager elsewhere, or a former trainee who mentors people you will never meet. Your organization may receive no direct financial benefit, yet its investment continues producing value. Traditional performance dashboards rarely capture that contribution.

Our paper argues that measuring educational outcomes only at graduation or the first job can overlook changes that emerge much later, including leadership, entrepreneurship and upward mobility. The same applies to professional development. A program evaluated after 12 months may reveal little about the influence its participants eventually have on others. Leaders should consider staying connected with former employees and tracking how their contributions evolve, without treating their subsequent achievements as corporate property.

The Foundation offers its framework as a starting point, not a definitive answer. We hope other scholarship providers and universities will test it with larger groups and more rigorous comparisons. Business leaders need not adopt our terminology to apply the underlying principle.

When deciding whether an investment in people has succeeded, ask two questions: What did this person achieve, and what did they subsequently make possible for others? The second is harder to measure, and its benefits may never return directly to the organization that made the investment. But three decades after founding the Foundation, I have come to believe it may be the more important question.

When my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

I founded the William S.D. Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind. Over the next three decades, I watched scholars build careers, support families and, in many cases, create opportunities for others. This year, the Foundation sought to understand those outcomes more systematically. It surveyed and interviewed former scholars, publishing its findings in a white paper, Opening Doors Through Education. The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

The findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. Former scholars described how their education helped them build careers, improve their families’ circumstances and contribute to their communities. Many have also gone on to support others through mentoring, volunteering and philanthropy, extending the benefits of their education to people they may never have reached otherwise.

#5227. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

On Nov. 18, Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) added the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms. The listing covers the web interface of the Hyperliquid trading terminal at app.hyperliquid.xyz/trade. The HYPE token dropped to around $65.50 on the evening of Nov. 18, and it recovered to $68.79 by midday Nov. 19, according to TradingView data.

According to the entry, the company claims to provide digital asset trading services on the website, and it has no address on record. Hyperliquid is not licensed by the SFC, and it is suspected of operating a virtual asset trading platform in Hong Kong or actively promoting its services to the public, the regulator said.

In an accompanying warning, the SFC reminded investors that such platforms often lure users with "incredible investment opportunities." The SFC also reminded investors that clients of unlicensed platforms have no legal protection if a platform is hacked or misappropriates their assets.

On the same day, the Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority with seven recommendations on the country's new crypto rules. "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity," the group wrote.

On Nov. 16, two days before the SFC added Hyperliquid to the list, Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan spoke at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum. "Before the end of this year, we will introduce a bill to complete the regulatory perimeter," Chan said.

According to Chan, the bill will cover crypto dealers, custodians, advisers and asset managers. "Decentralisation does not mean less accountability," he said.

In April, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority licensed HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial as the first stablecoin issuers in the city, out of 36 applicants in the first round.

#5224. As AI Takes on More Work, a Leader’s Responsibility Only Grows. Here’s Why.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The pace of change is accelerating, and AI is reshaping how businesses work. But some things cannot be delegated to machines.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past few years, entrepreneurs have been living in a state of constant mobilization. First came the pandemic, followed by geopolitical instability, shifting markets, the emergence of artificial intelligence and a new generation of technology-driven competitors.

After several years of running this marathon, it might seem that we should finally be able to catch our breath. Yet it is precisely now that we are beginning to realize that the pace of change is only accelerating.

We have become accustomed to looking for ways to manage stress: exercise, saunas, digital detoxes and meditation. But perhaps the problem is not simply how much time we spend resting. Perhaps the pace of change itself has fundamentally shifted.

The defining feature of our time is the exponential development of technology. Today, we are no longer talking simply about digitalization, but about the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence. AI is ceasing to be a standalone tool and is beginning to shape the environment in which businesses operate. It accelerates analysis, automates processes, changes consumer expectations and reduces the cost of many operations.

But as opportunities grow, so does human responsibility.

In the past, a company could operate for years based on a strategy chosen once and then followed consistently. Today, almost every change becomes a separate project: introducing artificial intelligence, modifying a product, restructuring sales channels or adapting to new customer habits. Entrepreneurs are no longer simply making decisions; they are constantly managing change.

Uncertainty is increasingly becoming the environment in which businesses are built. The question for every entrepreneur is whether they can make decisions and take action under such conditions.

I often say that entrepreneurship is not so much a profession as a state of mind. Education, planning and capital all help, but entrepreneurs must act with incomplete information, adapt, overcome setbacks and maintain the emotional balance required to lead others.

This is precisely why emotional intelligence matters so much. Strong analysts can be hired, but a leader must personally learn to manage their own reactions, understand others and communicate convincingly in stressful situations.

A team takes its cues from its leader. If the leader freezes, the organization slows down. If they act recklessly, it risks losing discipline. The challenge is to remain calm without becoming passive, and optimistic without ignoring risks.

Persistence is equally important: that inner drive that keeps you working until you achieve the desired result. At the same time, the tools and the route may change. It is important not to confuse persistence with stubbornness, or activity with actual progress.

The paradox is that as AI takes over more routine tasks, the responsibility of leaders continues to grow. It is the human being who determines the direction of development, builds the team and assesses strategic risks. The ability to understand what is happening and adapt more quickly is therefore becoming a key competitive advantage.

A leader can only step away from the controls when there are people around them capable of taking over. This makes one of the most important resources available to any leader the ability to build a strong team, establish trust with partners and delegate authority.

But there is a question that I believe is far more important than efficiency.

We talk far too often about how to outperform competitors, increase market capitalization or scale a business. Almost never do we ask ourselves a different question: What is the ultimate purpose of being human?

You can defeat your competitors, build the largest company and achieve extraordinary results. Yet none of these things guarantees what matters most: a happy life.

Most people define their goals in terms of achievements. Almost nobody says: My primary goal is to build the happiest possible life for myself. Yet this is precisely the goal that determines the value of all other achievements!

Inner exhaustion is not always simply a matter of how much work we do. If the lifestyle we have chosen consistently leads to it, we should ask ourselves what goals we are pursuing. Perhaps something needs to change.

So perhaps the most useful advice for entrepreneurs today is surprisingly simple: Start by understanding yourself. Understand your genuine emotional needs, strengths, natural abilities and limitations. Do not try to become someone you are not. Do not build a career that goes against your own nature.

People generally enjoy doing things they are good at. And they tend to become good at things they genuinely enjoy doing. When these two things coincide, the likelihood of success increases significantly.

This applies beyond business. Even philanthropy, traditionally regarded as an exclusively altruistic activity, naturally benefits the person who gives as well. The opportunity to share knowledge, help others and see the results of one’s actions all generate positive emotions. There is nothing wrong with that. It is simply human nature.

In general, many things become easier to understand when viewed through the lens of biology rather than conventional abstractions. Our emotions, motivation and sense of fulfillment have a very real physiological basis. Relationships with other people, meaningful work, the environment in which we live, our health and our ability to take pleasure in our own achievements — these are the elements that combine to create a sense of well-being.

Happiness, therefore, is neither a matter of luck nor a state of constant euphoria. It is a dynamic balance between the emotions a person genuinely needs and the states they experience at any given moment. This balance cannot be found once and preserved forever. It must be maintained continuously, with adjustments to our lives as the world around us changes.

And perhaps this is one of the greatest challenges of the age of artificial intelligence.

Machines may become increasingly capable of analyzing data, writing code, creating content, automating processes and helping us make decisions. But help with a decision is not the same as responsibility for it. The question of why we are in business and what kind of life we want to live remains ours to answer.

That is why a leader’s true competitive advantage lies not only in the ability to use AI, but also in the ability to remain the author of their own life.

Technology may change the rules of the game many times over. The pace of change may accelerate, and artificial intelligence may take over a significant share of intellectual work. But responsibility for our own decisions, our own happiness and our own path will remain with us.

And perhaps this is the most valuable skill a leader can possess today: the ability to maintain inner strength and remain the author of their own life, even as the world around them changes faster than ever before.

Over the past few years, entrepreneurs have been living in a state of constant mobilization. First came the pandemic, followed by geopolitical instability, shifting markets, the emergence of artificial intelligence and a new generation of technology-driven competitors.

After several years of running this marathon, it might seem that we should finally be able to catch our breath. Yet it is precisely now that we are beginning to realize that the pace of change is only accelerating.

We have become accustomed to looking for ways to manage stress: exercise, saunas, digital detoxes and meditation. But perhaps the problem is not simply how much time we spend resting. Perhaps the pace of change itself has fundamentally shifted.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin and Ethereum are bouncing back after a brutal selloff, but the recovery is running into a market that still looks far from healthy. Bitcoin climbed back above $60,000 over the weekend after touching a low near $55,250. Ethereum also gained ground, its first breath of air after several days of relentless selling, a good day for crypto despite bad news and uncertainty.

U.S. stocks suffered another heavy selloff on Friday, with the Nasdaq losing more than 5% as people questioned AI valuations and spending. Asian markets followed lower today, while Bitcoin recovered. Crypto buyers are stepping in, though it doesn’t yet signal that risk appetite has returned.

Crypto will face a tougher test as traditional markets reopen. We are watching technology stocks, oil prices, Treasury yields, and Federal Reserve expectations for clues. A lasting turnaround would need more than short-covering and bargain hunting. It needs buyers willing to hold positions while uncertainty remains high.

The bounce followed a sharp liquidation wave that dragged Bitcoin toward $55,000, its lowest level since September 2024. Yet, this kind of flush can create room for a rebound. Forced sellers disappear, short positions begin closing, and investors who waited on the sidelines see more attractive entry prices.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs are still recording outflows, including a $582 million withdrawal at the end of the week. BlackRock’s IBIT alone suffered $541 million in outflows during the session.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to turn $60,000 into support rather than another rejection. Holding above that psychological level would improve its short-term structure. A move toward $62,000 would give bulls a more meaningful foothold, while a drop toward the recent low would put the recovery in jeopardy.

Ethereum faces a similar challenge, but its performance against Bitcoin matters just as much as its dollar price. If ETH begins outperforming BTC, it could signal that traders are becoming comfortable taking on additional risk. If Bitcoin leads while Ethereum remains weak, the market may still be hiding in the safest corner of crypto even if we see news and catalysts from geopolitics.

The bigger threat to the recovery may come from outside the crypto market. Friday’s selloff hammered technology stocks, sending the Nasdaq down 5.3% and pushing the S&P 500 into correction territory. Investors are questioning AI spending and if it can justify enormous valuations, creating pressure across risk assets.

Bitcoin has increasingly behaved like a high-beta technology trade during periods of stress. When people reduce exposure to growth stocks, crypto gets caught in the same wave. A stabilization in Nasdaq trading could provide an important tailwind, especially if investors begin buying beaten-down technology shares again.

Oil offers another important signal as Brent crude hovers around $92 a barrel, and WTI trades at $83. Both benchmarks had fallen during the previous week, and lower oil prices could help ease inflation pressure, potentially giving the Federal Reserve more flexibility and reducing pressure on bond yields. That would improve conditions for assets sensitive to liquidity.

BREAKING: US stock market futures rebound as markets reopen for the first time since the Nasdaq 100's worst week since 2020:1. S&P 500: +1.4%2. Nasdaq 100: +2.2%3. Dow Jones: +0.9%4. WTI Crude: +1.5%5. Gold: +2.0%S&P 500 futures are back above 7000.

Gold also rebounds after suffering its steepest weekly decline since March. Bullion rose as traders reassessed interest-rate expectations, but its recovery remains fragile. If gold, stocks, and crypto begin stabilizing together, combined with good geopolitical news, it would suggest forced selling is easing across markets. If equities continue falling, temporary rebounds might disappear quickly.

Today, Bitcoin and Ethereum are showing signs of life, not confirmation of a new trend. Bitcoin needs to hold its reclaimed levels, ETF demand must improve, and Wall Street needs to stop bleeding. Until those pieces fall into place, this bounce may be the market catching its breath rather than preparing for another rally.

#5220. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

#5219. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

Blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

Databricks, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based SaaS business that’s built on top of a bunch of open source tools, has raised a massive $400 million in Series F funding at a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion valuation. Today’s funding brings the total raised to almost a $900 million. Andreessen Horowitz led the round with new investors BlackRock,  T. Rowe Price Associates, and Tiger Global Management also participating. TechCrunch has more here.

IonQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based startup that uses charged particles suspended in a vacuum, as the basis for its hardware, has raised $55 million in funding. Samsung and Mubadala Capital co-led the round, joined by Amazon, GV, and New Enterprise Associates. Fortune has more here.

Aurora Insight, a three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based startup that provides a “dynamic” global map of wireless connectivity that it built and monitors in real time using AI combined with data from sensors on satellites, vehicles, buildings, aircraft and other objects, has raised $18 million in Series A funding. Alsop Louie Partners and True Ventures co-led the round,  joined by Tippet Venture Partners, Rise of the Rest Seed Fund, Promus Ventures, Alumni Ventures Group, ValueStream Ventures, and Intellectus Partners. TechCrunch has more here.

Benevity, an 11-year-old, Calgary, Alberta-based company that makes corporate social responsibility and employee engagement software, has raised $30.5 million in Series C funding from General Atlantic and JMI Equity. More here. EV Connect, a 10-year-old, L.A.-based company that sells software to manage electric vehicle charging, has raised $12 million in a Series B round led by Mitsui & Co. and Ecosystem Integrity Fund. The company has raised $25 million to date. TechCrunch has more here.

Octave, a year-old, San Francisco-based tech-based behavioral health practice, has raised $11 million in Series A funding led by Greycroft, with participation from Obvious Ventures and earlier backers. The company has raised at least $14 million to date. Crunchbase News has more here.Signal AI, a six-year-old, London-based business intelligence and media monitoring startup, has raised $25 million in Series C funding. Redline Capital led the round, joined by MMC Ventures, GMG Ventures, and Hearst Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

AllWork, a 3.5-year-old, New York-based on-demand work platform that’s targeting large enterprise customers in need of temporary workers, has raised $3.8 million in seed funding from Great Oaks, Lightspeed Scout Fund, The Fund, Fernbrook, SmartHub, and numerous angel investors. More here.

Beem, a year-old, Boston-based CBD company that’s marketing its branded oils, protein bars, and a salve to athletes who may be looking for alternatives to chemically derived pain relievers and anti-inflammatories, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by Obvious Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Intrepida Bio, a newly launched, San Diego-based biotech focused on modulating innate immune systems, has raised $9.5 million from Sofinnova and Canaan Partners. FierceBiotech has more here.

LabGenius, a seven-year-old, London-based startup that’s applying AI and robotic automation to protein drug discovery, has raised $10 million in Series A funding. The round was led by Lux Capital and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Felicis Ventures, Inovia Capital, Air Street Capital and earlier investors, along with numerous notable individuals. TechCrunch has more here.

Margin Edge, a four-year-old, Falls Church, Va.-based maker of restaurant management software, has raised $5 million in Series A funding led by Osage Venture Partners, with participation from Good Company. More here.

Medinas, a two-year-old, Berkeley, Ca.-based company that helps healthcare organizations resell their surplus medical equipment and supplies, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by NFX. Additional investors in the round include Precursor Ventures, Sound Ventures, FJ Labs and Bryan Frist (of HCA Healthcare’s founding family). Crunchbase News has more here.

MediView XR, a two-year-old, Cleveland, Oh.-based medical device company working on a surgical navigation system that leverages augmented reality and spatial computing to provide surgeons with advanced visualization, has raised $4.5 million in seed funding. Backers include Inside View Investment,Plug and Play Ventures and Northwest Ohio Tech Fund. More here.

Reibus, a year-old, Atlanta, Ga.-based online marketplace for industrial materials, has raised $3.25 million in seed funding led by Bowery Capital, with participation from Initialized Capital and Stage 2 Capital. More here.

Marcelo Claure, the chief operating officer of SoftBank Group, will assume the position of executive chairman of the board of directors of WeWork when the company receives a planned $1.5 billion payment from SoftBank. TechCrunch has more here.

John Donahoe, the current president and CEO of ServiceNow, is taking over as the CEO and president of Nike in January, replacing Mark Parker who has been since 2006 and lived through numerous controversies over the years. Donahoe knows Nike well, having joined its board, where he will retain a seat, since 2014. In the meantime, Parker will become the company’s executive chairman and Bill McDermott, who abruptly resigned as the longtime CEO of SAP earlier this month for reasons that weren’t clear, is taking over as CEO of ServiceNow. The company’s shareholders apparently prefer Donahoe, who is also the chairman of PayPal and a former CEO of eBay, which he led from 2008 through 2015. At least, shares of ServiceNow dropped in price on the news.

Zaz Floreani has joined the Austin-based venture firm Next Coast Ventures as a principal. Floreani was most recently the VP of corporate development at the same-day delivery company Dropoff. More here.

Manuel Henriquez, founder and former CEO of Hercules Growth Technology Capital, and his wife Elizabeth have both pleaded guilty for their roles in the college admissions cheating scandal. She is to be sentenced Feb. 7 and her husband on March 5. The San Jose Mercury News has more here.

Why the Oscars, Emmys and Tonys are not ready for they and them.

A machine-learning system that’s betting the Astros will win the World Series (though our money is still on the Nats).

#5218. Binance to Remove Five Crypto Trading Pairs in 24 Hours: Countdown Begins

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Binance will delist five crypto spot trading pairs within the next 24 hours on Nov. 20, 2026, following a review.

To protect its users and to ensure a high-quality trading market, Binance conducts regular reviews of all listed spot trading pairs; it may delist certain spot trading pairs for various reasons, including low liquidity and trading volume.

Binance will delist GAS/TRY, HBAR/BNB, HIVE/TRY, KSM/TRY and ZAMA/TRY pairs on November 20, 2026 at 03:00 UTC, according to an official announcement published on November 18.

Four of the five affected pairs are related to the Turkish lira (TRY), while the last one is HBAR/BNB. The decision affects trading between these specific assets and does not mean the cryptocurrencies themselves are being completely delisted from Binance.

The exchange clarified that users will still be able to trade the affected tokens through other available spot trading pairs on its platform.

Binance will terminate Spot Trading Bots services for the spot trading pairs simultaneously where applicable. Users are strongly advised to update and/or cancel their Spot Trading Bots prior to the cessation of services for Spot Trading Bots to avoid any potential losses.

In related news, Binance Margin will initiate a routine cleanup of Cross Margin accounts with collateral valued at less than 1 USD (or equivalent in other assets), effective from November 30, 2026 at 00:00 (UTC). The cleanup will be executed on a daily basis as an ongoing operational process.

Affected accounts include Cross Margin Accounts with a collateral value of less than 1 USD equivalent across all assets and no outstanding liabilities, as well as Margin Accounts with no capital activity in the past 6 months. Capital activity refers to any action that generates a capital flow.

For each eligible Small-Asset Account, the system will automatically transfer the collateral in users’ Margin Accounts to their Spot Accounts while the Margin Account functions remain normal, allowing users to transfer, borrow, or trade at any time after the cleanup.

Accounts with collateral equal to or exceeding 1 USD equivalent are not affected by this cleanup.

#5215. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

Updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

Tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a new factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.)

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”

#5213. XRP Outperforms Solana and Dogecoin in Japan

Although XRP is at risk of losing its top-four position in the global cryptocurrency market, the asset still ranks among the three largest crypto assets in Japan.

In a recent post shared by the renowned Ripple-backed XRP treasury firm Evernorth, the company highlighted XRP’s growing performance in the Japan crypto market.

Earlier today, Evernorth shared monthly data from the Japan Virtual and Crypto Assets Exchange Association (JVCEA) revealing that XRP recorded about ¥132.8 billion in spot trading volume in September 2026.

While this accounted for about 15% of Japan's total crypto spot trading volume during the month, XRP emerged as the third most-traded cryptocurrency in Japan after Bitcoin and Ethereum.

This shows that XRP has outperformed other major altcoins that are currently trading in the Japan crypto market, hitting about $880 million in trading volume.

While further data showed Solana and Dogecoin ranking next to XRP on the list as the fourth- and fifth-largest cryptocurrencies in Japan, respectively, the data also showed a wide gap from XRP’s ¥132.8 billion spot volume.

This means that XRP is significantly ahead of Solana and Dogecoin in the Japan crypto trading market, as Solana recorded only about ¥19.47 billion in trading volume during the same month.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, saw less participation, as it recorded only ¥11.27 billion in spot volume during the same period.

With XRP sitting in the third spot, the asset has become one of the most actively traded cryptocurrencies in Japan despite its persistent price volatility.

#5212. Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.)

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5211. What’s Coming for Solana in 2027? Upgrade Planned Across Four Key Areas

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

At the 2026 Breakpoint event, Brennan Watt, CEO of Anza, gave a walkthrough of Solana’s wins this year, while sharing what is in store for 2027.

According to Watt, 2026 was a major year for Solana as it migrated its consensus to Alpenglow, slashed the block times in half from 400 ms to 200 ms while doubling capacity.

The Alpenglow upgrade went live on mainnet on October 21, 2026, cutting transaction finality from about 12.8 seconds down to roughly 150 milliseconds. It replaced TowerBFT with Votor, a faster path to reaching agreement.

After Alpenglow, @bw_solana laid out @anza_xyz roadmap for Solana in 2027 Performance: network compute capacity doubles, transactions cut 80% CU units for token accounts Expressivity: vector processing for models running fully onchain, 64 → 96 accounts per transaction, read account data instead of copying it so less data moves per transaction Market Structure: Alpenglow. Next with faster block distribution and Constellation for clearer ordering rules and more competition among validators Resilience: simpler protocol with fewer special cases, safer to change https://t.co/EpvDdSyjln

Solana recently transitioned to 1.0, marking the network’s graduation from “mainnet beta” to “mainnet” and retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch. Solana 1.0 recognizes the progress on network performance, resilience, and developer experience.

According to Watt, Solana is eyeing significant improvements in 2027 across four categories. First is Resilience, which involves simplifying the protocol, reducing special cases, and making it safer to change.

“So, we're going to go ahead and simplify the protocol, replacing legacy abstractions and interfaces, pushing more of the execution on chain, and modernizing some of the wire formats. And all of this, you know, enhances resiliency, but it also allows us to move quicker and be more agile and deploy things and evolve the protocol more quickly,” Watt stated.

Second is Market Structure, which centers on Alpenglow, which aims for faster block distribution, and Constellation, which aims for clearer ordering rules and more competition among validators.

“Several important Alpenglow extensions are coming,” Watt stated. Alpenglow rolls out in two phases: first is Votor, its voting protocol, which is already live on the platform; second is Rotor, a single relay layer planned for a later release that will replace Turbine, the protocol that spreads a block’s data across the network.

Third is Performance, where network compute capacity doubles and transactions use 80% fewer compute units for token accounts. Last is Expressivity, which involves vector processing for models running fully onchain and an increase from 64 to 96 accounts per transaction.

Watt also spoke about improvements in onchain development: “The cost of storing data on Solana came down by 27% this year. And just in the coming two weeks, we're going to bring this thing down by another 7x.”
